💡 Key Takeaways
  • AI-powered workspaces are tech companies’ latest focus, as the industry still struggles to perfect adoption.
  • During the keynote for the firm’s Ignite conference on Tuesday, CEO Satya Nadella announced Copilot Workspaces, a collaborative, “multiplayer” surface for Copilot’s agentic capabilities.
  • Also: Microsoft notes its fresh AI coding model rivals Claude Opus 5.5 at 5% of the cost.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-powered workspaces are tech companies’ latest focus, as the industry still struggles to perfect adoption. Microsoft has just put its offering into the ring.

During the keynote for the firm’s Ignite conference on Tuesday, CEO Satya Nadella announced Copilot Workspaces, a collaborative, “multiplayer” surface for Copilot’s agentic capabilities.

Also: Microsoft notes its fresh AI coding model rivals Claude Opus 5.5 at 5% of the cost.

The product, available in Frontier for now, is similar to OpenAI’s ChatGPT Space and several new Anthropic features, including Whiteboard and Sheets, which essentially merge the work tools you’re used to using with an agentic framework.

Industry observers note that “As the evolution of Copilot Notebooks, it’s where people and agents build on each other’s work,” Microsoft said. “An agent drafts a section of a document, and you review. You leave a comment, and an agent picks it up.”.

Microsoft also declared Autopilot, a sort of counterpoint agent to Copilot that “can watch Teams channels, follow up on emails, run recurring work, and manage a project — without waiting for a prompt,” as Microsoft described.

In a demo video during the keynote, the agent appeared to function similarly to OpenAI’s Dots, but for work — employees can tag their Autopilot “like a colleague,” Microsoft mentioned, and assign it tasks.

Also: 4 ways Anthropic’s upcoming Claude Sheets beat using a Google Sheets connector.

Microsoft remarked the agent will be able to autonomously handle “meetings and follow-ups on its own,” though that claim may be best verified by teams themselves.

Speaking of trust, however, Microsoft noted that “Autopilot runs on the identity, security, and compliance foundation IT already uses,” and that “each Autopilot has its own Microsoft Entra Agent ID and a named manager,” meaning IT can block it as needed.

“Its sign-ins and actions are logged under its own name, so security teams have a clear audit trail. Powered by Work IQ, it understands how your organization works within existing permissions,” Microsoft remarked.

In a recent development, the tech giant added that employees will soon “be able to bring their personal Autopilot into Workspaces” as well. The feature is also available in Frontier.

According to recent reports, nadella also revealed a few other productivity features, including a “command center” called Today that spans email, calendar, meetings, tasks, and threads in Teams. Currently in private preview in Outlook and the Copilot app, it includes a personalized briefing and a feed of priorities that updates throughout the day.

“The draft is written and ready for you to edit; the schedule change is already proposed; and the forgotten follow-up is waiting for you to send it, complete with context so you can catch up swiftly,” Microsoft stated of the feature, which sounds like an agentic briefing-cum-morning-assistant.

Also: Nearly 70% of workers use AI regularly now – but many get no time to upskill.

In a recent development, microsoft also unveiled that Home, now generally available, unifies Chat and Cowork into a singular starting point. That’s similar to Anthropic’s recent consolidation of its chat and agentic Cowork offerings, demonstrating an overall trend toward simplification in workplace AI.

While more companies are finally starting to see a return on their AI investment, agents are still expensive and can promptly rack up costs when unsupervised.

Microsoft announced a few tools to track this at Ignite: Agent 365 Business Analytics and Agent 365 Cost Management.

Also: Microsoft wants to put a dollar value on AI’s work – but can you trust the math?

Sources indicate that agent 365, which Microsoft declared last year, is the firm’s observability platform. Microsoft remarked Business Analytics, in Frontier Public today, provides insights on what a company is spending on AI and why, and where it’s paying off, as well as forecasts future costs. In a demo during the keynote, Microsoft showed how admins can see when specific agents’ costs have spiked recently and what (human) employee to notify as a result.

Recent findings suggest that “It starts with a new way to measure your investment: in work completed, not simply tokens,” Microsoft noted. “It analyzes the tasks, how long that work typically takes a person, and the share Cowork performed, providing a sophisticated view of the hours your intelligence supports and what the work is worth.”.

Cost Management lets IT see where teams are using AI down to the model.

“Leaders can set spending policies, limits, and proactive alerts and control which models are available,” Microsoft noted. Anthropic released a similar tool last month, though it was focused more on making seats as efficient as possible on Teams and Enterprise plans.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • During the keynote at its Ignite conference on Tuesday, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella announced several fresh models from Microsoft AI (MAI), its lab within the company.
  • Also: Microsoft says its new AI coding model rivals Claude Opus 5.5.
  • MAI said it would allow its customers to customize its frontier models with their own data and run them securely in Azure through an initiative called Licensed Weights.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

During the keynote at its Ignite conference on Tuesday, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella announced several fresh models from Microsoft AI (MAI), its lab within the company. But new model releases are almost a dime a dozen these days, and accelerating fast — what really stood out was how Microsoft will let its customers access those models.

Also: Microsoft says its new AI coding model rivals Claude Opus 5.5.

MAI said it would allow its customers to customize its frontier models with their own data and run them securely in Azure through an initiative called Licensed Weights. It’s essentially a selective approach to open-weight AI: more so than proprietary models from OpenAI and Anthropic, but not fully downloadable on Hugging Face like Mistral’s Le Chonk. Interested companies will need to go through their Microsoft account reps to get started.

“You control who can access it. Your data and adaptations stay entirely yours. And we’ll work with you through Frontier Company to deliver the custom model and embed it in your own products and agents,” Mustafa Suleyman, CEO of MAI, remarked during the keynote.

According to recent reports, the approach should stand out to businesses looking for affordable AI that lets them retain control over their IP. Microsoft noted it would only use customers’ information to train its models if they agreed.

“No one wants to pour their IQ into someone else’s model,” Suleyman noted during the keynote, a nod to an argument Palantir CEO Alex Karp has made repeatedly.

The dominant, if simplified, narrative in AI has been that proprietary, expensive models boast peak capabilities but aren’t customizable, while open, cheaper models are customizable but less capable. Microsoft’s AI models don’t necessarily compete with OpenAI and Anthropic yet, but the manufacturer has legacy sway with countless businesses. By offering a customizable AI option, it could strike a balance among major tech companies.

Western labs, including Thinking Machines and Mistral, are releasing more competitive open-weight models, but Anthropic and OpenAI still have the overwhelming majority of the enterprise AI market. Though Licensed Weights isn’t an open-weight family of models, it does diversify the open-versus-closed debate a bit and differentiate Microsoft’s offering from OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s. It’s also a smart pairing with Microsoft’s goal to balance price and performance, if businesses find it impressive enough.

Also: Microsoft unveiled Copilot Workspaces at Ignite 2026.

“Averaged over four widely used benchmarks that target the everyday enterprise coding tasks we see in GitHub Copilot, MAI Code 2 gives you 98% of the performance of GPT 6.1 Sol at just 40% of the cost, and against Opus 5.5 it’s an incredible 5% of that cost,” Suleyman mentioned of the fresh coding model the manufacturer announced at Ignite.

Recent findings suggest that the firm also released its newly introduced image editing model, MAI Image 2.7, on Tuesday, which now leads the category on Artificial Analysis while beating Nano Banana Pro and several GPT image models on price and quality. With Licensed Weights, Microsoft has positioned itself for organizations seeking a reliable blend of ROI tools, customization, security controls, and capability.

Industry News: We tested 7 rugged tablets – these 2 outlasted the cold and heat best

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (971 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Zdnet

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For some, a tablet is a lightweight e-reader, or a more portable way to browse the web, take notes, and stream movies.
  • Industry observers note that rugged tablets differ from regular tablets in that they are usually military-grade certified for durability and can operate in more extreme temperatures.
  • ZDNET’s lab in Louisville, KY, tested seven tablets from brands like Samsung, Dell, and more, by putting them in frigid-cold and sweltering-hot conditions to see how their battery life would hold up.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For some, a tablet is a lightweight e-reader, or a more portable way to browse the web, take notes, and stream movies. For others, a tablet is a capable and durable device that needs to withstand outdoor conditions like fieldwork, camping, or construction sites. In these instances, you’ll need a rugged tablet.

Also: The best rugged tablets you can buy.

Industry observers note that rugged tablets differ from regular tablets in that they are usually military-grade certified for durability and can operate in more extreme temperatures. Since their build and intent are different from regular tablets, we decided to develop a upcoming test to compare rugged tablets and their performance capabilities.

ZDNET’s lab in Louisville, KY, tested seven tablets from brands like Samsung, Dell, and more, by putting them in frigid-cold and sweltering-hot conditions to see how their battery life would hold up. Based on our extensive testing, the Samsung Galaxy Tab Active 5 Pro won our cold test, and the Oukitel RT10 won our hot test.

Sources indicate that to test these tablets, we first needed to test their baseline battery life. Gianmarco Chumbe, our lab’s product testing manager, battery-tested these tablets at room temperature (72°F) with the following configurations: screens set to ~500 nits of brightness, Airplane Mode on, a looped playback of the same 1080p H.264 video file (no audio track) in VLC, and the system audio muted. Each tablet started out at 100% battery.

To document battery degradation, a lightweight Python script ran on each tablet throughout the test and logged the battery level every minute. For Windows tablets — like the Dell Pro Rugged models — it read the battery status via the psutil library. Android tablets like the Samsung Galaxy Tab Active 5 Pro used the Termux app to read the battery status via the Termux API. Each tablet plays the looped video, with logging running, until playback stops. We found that Windows tablets were set to shut down at their critical battery level, and Android tablets entered a dormant state at about 1%.

According to recent reports, after getting the baseline results above, Chumbe focused on our cold test, which consisted of placing each tablet in a consumer freezer set to -6°F and running the same configuration as above to simulate a harsh winter environment. Battery life drops were documented once per minute — the same as the baseline test.

The heat test required a more complex setup: Chumbe created a “tablet sauna” using a 40 × 20 × 20-inch enclosure with walls made of half-inch PVC board and a quarter-inch acrylic front panel for viewing the tablets during testing. A 400 Watt fan-forced PTC heater sat at one end of the chamber, while a 20 × 12-in aluminum baffle, positioned 10 inches in front of the heater, blocked its direct airflow, so no tablet was directly heated by it. A circulation fan ran continuously to keep the air evenly mixed.

The thermostat was set between 104 and 106°F, with the heater cycling roughly every 2 minutes (30 seconds on and 90 seconds off). A second, independent thermostat cut power to the heater if the air reached 115°F, protecting the units if the main thermostat failed. Finally, a single 1 ⅛-in. port, sealed around the cables, carried the power and sensor cords. Again, the same configurations and documentation process were used.

Also: How we test tablets at ZDNET in 2026.

In a recent development, some caveats to keep in mind about our testing: the test temperatures reflect the surrounding air, not the device temperature, and while every tablet ran the same video at the same measured brightness, the screen size, panel, processor, and battery capacity differ for each tablet tested. Runtimes reflect each tablet as sold and aren’t normalized for battery size.

As you can see from Fig. 1 above, the Samsung Galaxy Tab Active 5 Pro won our cold test, lasting 12 hours and 47 minutes at -6°F. An honorable mention goes to the Oukitel RT10, which remained at 1% battery for one hour.

Read the reviews: Samsung Galaxy Tab Active 5 Pro | Oukitel RT10.

Sources indicate that an interesting result we had was that neither of the Dell Rugged Tablets completed our cold test. The Dell Pro Rugged 12 Tablet tapped out at 5.10 hours at 78% battery, and the Dell Pro Rugged 10 Tablet stopped working after 6.23 hours at 67% battery. Both tablets displayed “Extreme cold T detected, shutting down for safety.”.

In a recent development, according to Dell’s official operating manual, both tablets should be able to withstand temperatures as low as -20.2°F. Dell states in its manual that performance can be reduced once temperatures reach 5°F, but the whole point of rugged tablets is to withstand harsh elements without needing to move to a warmer area for them to work.

ZDNET reached out to Dell to comment on these results, and we will patch this story once they respond.

In our heat test, the tablet that lasted the longest in our tablet sauna was the Oukitel RT10, which persisted for 32.07 hours. And even though the Dell Pro Rugged tablet didn’t complete our cold test, it came in second for our heat test and lasted 21.65 hours.

As you can see from both Fig. 1 and Fig. 2, the DT Research Rugged Tablet DT312RP had the worst-performing battery out of both tests; however, it wasn’t far off from its original baseline result of 4.43 hours, and even outperformed that baseline number in the heat test (4.65 hours).

Our test results might differ from your own experiences with these tablets, especially depending on the temperature at which you use them and the applications/connections you have running. However, as a benchmark, our testing provides real-world results on how different rugged tablets can handle extreme conditions.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I want you to understand just how much money this tech giant rakes in.

I want you to understand just how much money this firm rakes in.

If someone handed you $8,300 every second, what would you do? That’s how much pure profit Nvidia now makes. By the time you finish reading this paragraph, Nvidia will likely have cleared $45,000 and change.

According to recent reports, it’s easy to look at Nvidia, a company that just lost its visionary founder CEO due to a series of scandals, and think that the company and maybe the entire AI industry are in terrible trouble. Perhaps so?

It has been revealed that but I want you to understand: Nvidia isn’t your average semi-successful tech giant that might tempt a newly introduced CEO to fix things that are broken. It is a company so staggeringly, mind-bogglingly successful it’ll do everything in its power not to rock the boat. There is so much money at stake.

It’s so much money that when I heard about Jensen Huang’s resignation, my first thought was: I need a way to visualize this jaw-dropping amount of money for you. I want to show you that Nvidia has risen so far, so fast, that rival chipmakers AMD, Intel, and Qualcomm barely qualify as competition now.

If you’re on a desktop OS, you could mouse over each dot in our chart above to see the staggering sums. But we built another way to visualize the rise of Nvidia I like even better. It’s a horizontal bar graph that not only puts Nvidia’s revenue growth in perspective, but indicates you its monster profits right alongside them — plus the world events that made Nvidia a star.

Recent findings suggest that TL;DR: The crypto boom and the great GPU shortage have nothing on the AI boom. Those earlier periods saw Nvidia’s profits briefly peak at $1.24 billion and $3 billion a quarter respectively, while the rise of data centers has driven them to $65 billion per quarter with no sign of stopping.

Yes, Jensen may have set a trillion dollars of Nvidia’s market cap on fire — from around $5 trillion at the start of November to “only” $3.6 trillion now — but the smoldering tech giant is raking in $700 million in profit a day on average.

Put another way: Nvidia could give a $1 million bonus to every one of its 42,000 employees, every three months, without running out of cash. Or, you know, Nvidia could end world hunger or provide clean water for everyone, now that it’s making over $200 billion in pure profit a year.

Maybe that’d make people feel differently about data centers?

Industry observers note that but even if we stick to self-serving capitalism, you’re probably still a happy investor if you bought Nvidia a decade ago. A $1,000 investment 10 years ago is now worth over $67,000. You’d have over $1 million if you invested $15,000 back then.

It has been revealed that and make no mistake, Nvidia is sticking to capitalism. Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress just promised to return as much money to investors as possible on the organization’s November 17th earnings call. “Going forward, we intend to return all excess free cash flow net of strategic uses to shareholders,” she announced. “All” is a lot more than the 50 percent baseline that Jensen promised five months ago.

Nvidia isn’t the only firm whose fortunes have risen this dramatically. RAMageddon revealed that just three companies — Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron — controlled nearly 90 percent of the entire global DRAM market, and those three have repeatedly signaled that they’d prefer to celebrate record profits instead of ramping up production too fast.

Industry observers note that but while their revenues and profits have been skyrocketing even faster over the past year or so, even Big RAM hasn’t caught the AI wave quite the same way as Nvidia. Samsung, of course, doesn’t just make memory — its revenue numbers include phones, tablets, TVs, home appliances, chips, displays, camera sensors, audio, networking equipment, medical equipment, and more.

Sources indicate that in the most recent quarter, Micron made $37.7 billion in profit, SK Hynix made $29.8 billion, and Samsung came in at around $55.3 billion, but they’re all shy of Nvidia’s $65.3 billion. Historically, RAM has also been a bit more cyclical: Both Micron and SK Hynix actually lost money in 2023 because they produced too much memory.

On its latest earnings call, the first since cofounder Jensen Huang’s resignation, interim CEO and CFO Colette Kress reinforced the idea that Nvidia expects the good times to keep on rolling.

Recent findings suggest that asked how things might change under new management, she suggested that they wouldn’t: “From a business perspective, it’s business as usual,” she said. She added that the company has secured the backing of customers and suppliers including TSMC, the all-vital firm that actually fabricates Nvidia’s chips.

It has been revealed that “Our momentum is real, our demand is accelerating, our supply is growing. Our customers and partners are with us, and employees are committed,” she claimed. “We’ve got this.”.

Industry observers note that nvidia claims it’ll rake in even more money next quarter, with projected revenue of $130 billion. Profit may be proportionally smaller since gross margins are estimated to drop to 71–72 percent (compared to nearly 75 percent), but Kress said Nvidia intends to get them up as high as 73 percent next year.

In other words: This astounding gravy train isn’t going anywhere. At least that’s the proposal.

Stevie Bonifield contributed to this story.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that morning Minute is a daily newsletter written by Tyler Warner. The analysis and opinions expressed are his own and do not necessarily reflect those of Decrypt. And check out our daily news show 'FOMO HOUR' covering all of the top stories and market action.

🏛️ Backpack and tZERO Win the First Onchain Derivatives Approvals.

For years, perps were the product American traders couldn’t legally touch. On Monday, that officially changed.

Industry observers note that chairman Michael Selig approved applications from Backpack and tZERO to run regulated derivatives exchanges and clearinghouses that execute and settle on blockchain rails. Selig called it “an vital milestone in the evolution of American financial markets.”.

Recent findings suggest that backpack got both pieces at once, a Designated Contract Market designation to run the exchange and a Derivatives Clearing Organization registration to clear its own trades. It aims to offer Americans round-the-clock leveraged crypto perps on a single global order book, accepting both fiat and crypto as collateral with cross-margin across positions. tZERO received its exchange approval a week earlier, after already holding clearing registration, and is building it into a derivatives vertical inside its infrastructure business.

Backpack US president Mark Wetjen, himself a former CFTC commissioner, framed it as “moving price discovery from offshore unregulated venues to the United States.” CEO Armani Ferrante said the firm enters markets “fully regulated from day one.” Backpack already runs licensed platforms in Europe, Asia and the UAE.

In a recent development, the CFTC has certainly been busy this month. They cleared single-stock perpetual futures on November 3. It issued guidance on November 5 telling federally regulated exchanges they generally cannot restrict access by state. Now it has approved blockchain-native exchanges and clearinghouses.

Selig is building an onshore home for every product the offshore venues were built to serve, and he is doing it through staff action rather than legislation, with one sitting commissioner and nomination hearings for two more this week.

According to recent reports, hyperliquid is the obvious candidate and also the one that has publicly said it doesn’t want this. Jeff Yan spent his Bloomberg interview this month arguing Hyperliquid is infrastructure rather than an exchange, and that regulators should oversee the firms deploying markets on top rather than the chain underneath. His US route is HIP-3 partners taking on the compliance burden, with ICE investing in Trade.xyz and Kraken’s parent reportedly in talks. Backpack getting a DCM and a DCO makes that argument harder, because it demonstrates a crypto-native venue can simply register.

Then there’s Lighter. It has run Robinhood Wallet’s perps since July on a dedicated instance with a 50/50 revenue split, which is the partner model rather than the registration model. The registered model opens up with a CFTC license, and many think Lighter could very well be next.

One thing’s certain—the CFTC is serious about bringing perps onshore. From Selig himself, “I look forward to building on that milestone.” And we will find out soon enough who’s next….

Outside the airport, hundreds of protesters packed streets bearing signs — and at least one prop casket — saying “Trump out.” Others say “Reject Pax Silica,” the name for the US-led international initiative to secure chips and critical minerals used in the hardware fueling the AI boom.

According to recent reports, “Pax” comes from the Latin word for “peace, stability, and long-term prosperity,” the Pax Silica website proudly notes. Yet the unspoken question — peace and prosperity for whom? — explains the whiplash between the Philippine government’s warm welcome of Trump and the public fury raging outside.

Recent findings suggest that trump states he wants to “win AI” — whatever that means. As such, the US needs data centers full of GPUs to do it. With Americans increasingly opposed to data centers and chip factories being built in their communities, the US is now recruiting less affluent nations to take up some of the slack. Lawmakers from both the US and the Philippines are promising a slice of the riches that advances in generative AI are supposed to create. And that’s supposed to be worth the land razed, homes destroyed, and natural resources lost in the name of technological progress. In the Philippines, that’s taking the shape of a proposed 1,620-hectare (4,000 acres) hub for chip factories, processing plants for critical minerals, and data centers.

At least two dozen countries have signed on to the Pax Silica initiative, and Trump was expected to pressure more to join while in the Philippines for events related to the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit. With Pax Silica, the US aims to insulate itself from China’s dominance in manufacturing semiconductors and processing critical minerals needed to make those chips. Trump held a bilateral meeting with President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. Wednesday before heading to Shenzhen to meet with China’s President Xi Jinping and Russia’s President Vladimir Putin.

It has been revealed that philippine and US officials are expected to sign a framework agreement by the end of the year for the jointly developed Pax Silica Economic Security Zone. The details are still murky and shrouded in NDAs. The Philippines’ Bases Conversion and Development Authority (BCDA) overseeing the plan expects an economic boom from minerals processing and chip manufacturing, with perhaps a data center or two on site. Meanwhile, human rights advocates who oppose the project warn that it will displace Indigenous residents, cutting them off from water resources on which they rely.

“How do we give up our burial grounds, our church, our livelihood?”.

It has been revealed that “We do not want to give up our community,” Petronila Capiz-Muñoz, chieftain of the Indigenous Aeta Hungey tribe, told Human Rights Watch. “How do we give up our burial grounds, our church, our livelihood? This is where we source our water, this is where we plant.” Capiz-Muñoz said BCDA officials have told residents that they’ll need to relocate by December to make way for development. Small farmers are also afraid the semiconductor hub will push them off their lands, according to Lian Buan, Southeast Asia researcher at Human Rights Watch.

There are layers of land-grabbing to unpack here.

Industry observers note that the Aeta are among the first people to inhabit the Philippines, believed to have arrived around 30,000 years ago. And yet the Aeta Hungey tribe has been trying since 1994 to secure an official certificate recognizing its ancestral domain in one of the areas now facing industrial development. But since the tribe hasn’t been granted that certificate, the BCDA can still claim the AI hub will be built “outside titled ancestral domains.”.

Sources indicate that the agency says the project will be located on public land located at the former Clark Air Base built in the early 1900s when the Philippines was a US territory. The Philippine constitution now only allows its own citizens to own private land. But the BCDA can offer leases lasting as long as 99 years to foreign developers. The agency expects to rake in close to $1 billion USD (about 60 billion in PHP Peso) from lease income over the first 25 years.

There are layers of land-grabbing to unpack here.

Sources indicate that the BCDA was in talks with around 30 different companies interested in setting up shop in Clark’s proposed AI hub, then-BCDA President and CEO Joshua Bingcang told reporters in July. He couldn’t name names, he stated, because of NDAs — creating the same kind of opacity that has turned Americans against data centers on their home turf.

He did mention, however, that an American energy company was conducting a feasibility study into building a liquefied natural gas (LNG) line and plant to meet the hub’s enormous electricity demand. Bingcang called LNG a clean fuel, but that’s provably false. LNG is primarily methane, a smog-forming pollutant that is an even more potent greenhouse gas than carbon dioxide.

Recent findings suggest that bingcang said in September that the Philippine government wanted to invite Nvidia, TSMC, and Apple. While one or two data center developers had expressed interest, according to Bingcang, most of the companies interested were “high tech” manufacturing firms. He has also described chip manufacturing as a “clean” industry, echoing corporate spin that’s been around since the start of Silicon Valley.

At the first chip fabs in California, workers — many of them Filipino immigrants — donned “bunny suits” to assemble sensitive chips in environmentally controlled “clean rooms.” Little did they know that the gear they wore offered little protection against the harsh chemicals used in manufacturing, which also leaked out of storage tanks to contaminate soil and groundwater. When studies came out in the ’90s documenting disproportionately high rates of miscarriages among workers, companies pledged to phase out some of the chemicals linked to reproductive health risks. Around the same time, chip manufacturing started to move out of the US to Asia, where similar health problems stemming from the same chemicals cropped up even decades later.

Chipmakers say their fabs have gotten much safer over the years, in part because more work is automated. Even so, the BCDA estimates that the AI hub will create up to 190,000 direct jobs. The BCDA, White House, and Philippine’s Malacañang Palace did not immediately respond to questions from The Verge.

“I don’t want to date myself, but I knew your parents very well. They were great,” Trump told President Marcos during his visit. Marcos’ parents are estimated to have stolen up to $30 billion from government coffers over decades of rule before a people power movement ousted the current president’s father from the same office in the 1980s. But public memory, it seems, can be short.

Industry observers note that and skyrocketing demand for more powerful chips used for generative AI has raised fears among environmental and labor groups that history might repeat itself. Companies move fast and break things, leaving a toxic mess in their wake. And when Americans decide they’ve had enough in their own back yards, the industry sets up shop somewhere else where they think their customers aren’t paying attention and politicians are happy to look the other direction.

Best battery performance in hot environments.

Also: We tested 7 rugged tablets – these 2 outlasted the cold and heat best.

It has been revealed that this is one chubby tablet. / Manufacturer or Full Name/ZDNET.

This heavy-duty tablet can take a beating and continue running for days.

The RT10 weighs in at a chonky 1255g. To put that into perspective, the 13-inch M4 iPad Pro weighs a scant 523g. Given the RT10 is an 11-inch tablet, the 11-inch version of the same iPad only weighs 444g. The RT10 weighs nearly three times the iPad.

Of course, the iPad would shudder if you took it into the conditions the RT10 is built for.

According to recent reports, with the form factor out of the way, let’s talk about how I fared with the Oukitel RT10. After unboxing the tablet, I connected Android to my Google account and set up the usual features (fingerprint, etc). As with any Android device, it was incredibly easy.

I then went about my usual testing. The first thing I do with tablets and phones is see how responsive the UI is. In the case of the RT10, the Android UI was a bit sluggish.

Also: The best rugged tablets you can buy.

That aroused my curiosity. I decided to install a different homescreen launcher. To be specific, I went with O Launcher. Why did I do this? Primarily because O Launcher uses fewer system resources than most, I figured it might solve the tablet’s sluggishness.

Industry observers note that lo and behold, using O Launcher as my default solved that glitch. Now the RT10 runs like an absolute champ.

With speed no longer an matter, I put the tablet through the usual paces. Here are my conclusions:.

The big problem some users might have is the weight. The RT10 is as heavy as a tablet can be. What you have to remember, however, is that’s part of what makes Oukitel’s products so unique.

In a recent development, the RT10 is specifically made to thrive in tough conditions. Take this tablet to the beach, on a hike, to a construction site… it doesn’t matter because it’s got the oomph to stand up to just about anything you can throw at it.

Also: The best rugged phones in 2026: Tested by experts.

Industry observers note that another thing I really appreciate about the Oukitel tablets is that most of them ship with a handy (and very sturdy) kickstand. The kickstand has to be attached, and it adds to the weight, but it’s very much worth using.

Gotta love these beefy kickstands.

According to recent reports, you also get a hand strap you can attach. Both of these accessories are attached by way of screws, so they are rock solid. Lastly, there’s a carrying strap you can attach to the kickstand to make carrying the RT10 around easier.

Industry observers note that the Oukitel line of devices appeals to a certain cross-section of society. If you drive a Ford F150 to work and you come home caked in dirt or construction dust, this tablet is for you. If you’re a hiker or camper, ditto. As well, if you want a tablet with an absolutely massive battery, you could do a whole lot worse than the RT10.

If, on the other hand, you prefer a tablet that weighs nothing, looks like every other tablet being carried around, and you don’t like Android, this tablet is most certainly not for you.

#5049. Grok Build coding agent leaks oodles of confidential info, some belonging to SpaceXSI

📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1125 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

Grok Build coding agent leaks oodles of confidential info, some belonging to SpaceXSI

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1125 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Grok Build, the vibe-coding agent from SpaceXSI, is leaking data—some of it proprietary business information and other sensitive secrets—from thousands of its users, including the very same Elon Musk-owned tech giant that offers the platform, new research reveals.
  • Industry observers note that the information is revealed through links allowing Grok Build users to share their apps with others.
  • Industry observers note that research from security firm Claroc shows that the exposed data includes things like internal business plans, ad proposals, medical exam results, galley checklists from a celebrity cruise line, and employee names and ID numbers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Grok Build, the vibe-coding agent from SpaceXSI, is leaking data—some of it proprietary business information and other sensitive secrets—from thousands of its users, including the very same Elon Musk-owned tech giant that offers the platform, new research reveals.

Industry observers note that the information is revealed through links allowing Grok Build users to share their apps with others. Grok takes steps to randomize the URLs so only people who know the exact URL can access the data stored there. A design decision by developers of the platform, however, completely torpedoes that objective and makes it possible for anyone to enumerate thousands of live Grok Build projects. Except in rare cases, clicking those links opens the app and reveals all data associated with it.

Industry observers note that research from security firm Claroc shows that the exposed data includes things like internal business plans, ad proposals, medical exam results, galley checklists from a celebrity cruise line, and employee names and ID numbers. Ironically, some of the sensitive data comes from two-dozen apps built by SpaceXSI (the name of the now-merged SpaceX and xAI) itself. A small sampling of the documents revealed in the SpaceXSI apps—Claroc found 24 of them—include an onboarding initiative, marked confidential, for a latest member of SpaceXSI’s enterprise sales team, a sales territory map of 594 accounts, internal system addresses for sales team tools, and advertising proposals.

“We were shocked,” Claroc said in a Tuesday post. “The company that makes Grok had its own internal material open to anyone holding the link, and we had never been given it. Had the sales team bought a tool for this, it would have sat behind company sign-in, open only to the team. Built with AI, it went live open to anyone with the link.

It has been revealed that claroc notified SpaceXSI of the privacy spill on Sunday. When no one responded, a Claroc official took to X to tag both Musk and Grok Manager Matt Palmer about the threat. At the time this post went live almost all data remained available with one notable exception: the contents from the 24 SpaceXSI apps. All of them were exposing the information on Monday evening. SpaceXSI began removing the links within a few hours of Ars sending an email with questions for this article. At the time this post went live, links for all 24 apps returned an “app not found” error.

Recent findings suggest that claroc found sensitive data belonging to other Grok Build owners, some working for Fortune 500 companies and a defense contractor. Some of the affected organizations and data revealed includes:.

Asaf Aprozper, the co-founder and CTO of Claroc, remarked he’s in the process of notifying companies. After speaking to the CISO of the luxury cruise manufacturer, it “pulled in their whole security team as soon as we shared the findings and are already working to contain the Grok exposure.”.

Link sharing for Grok Build is intended to streamline the process of developing and deploying apps. A user can input speech or text and have a working app ready for internal testing within minutes. The links are designed to give developers a way to get the app in front of authorized people promptly. The very left of the URLs contain two or more “dice words,” meaning randomly generated phrases such as “failing chassis traders,” although users can modify them. The rightmost portion of the link is grok.me. The URL for an X ads campaign plan was: https://cinder-crane-sand-frost.grok.me.

In a recent development, the scheme is intended to prevent links from being easily guessable. When done correctly, a phrase comprising three dice words has roughly 38 bits of entropy, amounting to billions of possible combinations. The idea—sometimes called capability-based access control—is that possession of the URL serves as authorization to the resources behind it. Google has long used this technique to make URLs easy to share but hard to guess. A URL share on that platform might look like: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1BxiMVs0XRA5nFMdKvBdBZjgmUUqptlbs74OgvE2upms/edit.

Recent findings suggest that there’s a fatal flaw in the way SpaceXSI has implemented the mechanism. Instead of being to the right of the domain—as is the case with Google links—the randomness for Grok Build links is positioned to the left of it. That allows the links to be easily enumerated using passive DNS services. These services monitor central DNS lookup servers. When a server lookup requests the IP address of a previously never-before-seen URL, the transaction is captured in a publicly searchable database. Had Grok followed Google’s approach, the links would have been invisible to passive DNS searchers. Muse, the Meta agent that CEO Mark Zuckerberg noted was built from the ground up for security, recently suspended a link-sharing feature after it too was found leaking sensitive data.

According to recent reports, aprozper stated a passive DNS search returned 43,601 links ending in grok.me. Of them, more than 35,000, or nearly 95 percent, were public, meaning that clicking on the link opened the corresponding app and all data it stored. He said that tests he conducted over the past week showed that, by default, Grok sets links to “Anyone with the link.” Users have the option to change the setting to “invited users” or “only you.”.

A representative with Cursor, the AI coding service SpaceXSI recently acquired, remarked in an email that Grok Build “apps are private by default and nothing goes public unless the creator chooses to share it.” The representative said that competing coding agents from ChatGPT, Lovable, and Bolt also give consumers the ability to generate shareable links.

Aprozper’s tests contradict the representative’s statement. In all cases, Grok Build required owners to change anyone with the link to one of the other two options.

It has been revealed that the Cursor statement regarding other AI coding platforms is correct. Aprozper stated that app builders, including Lovable, Bolt, and Replit, “also give each app its own web address, so the same DNS records expose them, too. However, Grok is where we found by far the most sensitive manufacturer data.” That means that people using these other platforms are also at risk of exposing sensitive data through shared links. Interestingly, AI platforms that follow the correct sharing link practice include Claude’s published artifacts (claude.ai/public/artifacts/), ChatGPT’s shared conversations (chatgpt.com/share/), and Gemini (gemini.google.com/share/). For all three, the secret randomness is in the path, so DNS never sees it.

The representative didn’t respond to follow-up questions, including if SpaceXSI intentionally exposed the proprietary internal information, why the company removed the data after Ars asked about it, and if it planned to notify customers who also exposed similar types of information. Anyone using shareable links with Grok Build should choose the “invite others” option unless they intend to make an app widely available.

Best battery performance in cold environments.

Recent findings suggest that A couple of months ago I popped the SIM out of my Galaxy S25 Ultra and spent a few weeks with the rugged Galaxy XCover7. To go along with that durable phone, Samsung just released the Galaxy Tab Active5 Pro tablet, and I’ve been hiking, kayaking, and exploring with it for the past few weeks.

Also: We tested 7 rugged tablets – these 2 outlasted the cold and heat best.

The Tab Active5 Pro improves upon the Active4 Pro in a few areas requested by regular consumers, including stereo speakers, expanded RAM with an updated Qualcomm Snapdragon 7s Gen 3 processor, and significantly improved battery capacity with dual hot-swap capability.

As a trade-off, the rear camera resolution has been decreased from 13MP to 12MP, but it’s still perfectly capable of capturing documents and images while out in the field.

Manufacturer or Full Name/ZDNET.

Samsung improved its rugged tablet with stereo speakers and large hot-swappable batteries.

Recent findings suggest that with 10,100 mAh of battery capacity contained in two user-replaceable cells, the Galaxy Tab Active5 Pro is built to serve its role continuously. In our lab testing, its battery lasted 12 hours and 47 minutes in -6°F conditions, allowing it to win a ZDNET Lab Award.

In order to test the Tab Active5 Pro in the field, I took it on a fishing trip to a high mountain lake in Washington State. It turns out there was no longer a trail to the lake, so I navigated through the overgrown forest down extremely steep terrain to the pristine lake.

Also: The best rugged tablets you can buy: Expert tested.

I did not intend to test the tablet’s rugged durability since those kinds of extreme tests are not allowed with loaners, but the conditions present during my trek resulted in some hard falls, water immersion, and real-life field testing of the tablet. It survived unscathed and was a joy to use.

As a professional naval architect, I survey ships and work in shipyards, with electronic drawings guiding me. The rugged Tab Active devices have worked well for my teams and me in the past in shipyards in Florida and Washington.

Over the past couple of weeks, the large spike S Pen has worked flawlessly for navigating around and marking up drawings. I especially appreciate the secure storage silo in the protective case. The larger diameter of the S Pen made it easy to use with gloves on, and the display can be manipulated in glove mode.

In a recent development, three physical buttons on the bottom of the tablet, in landscape orientation, make it easy to unlock and navigate the user interface. A lime green button on the top, identified as the active button, can be customized with actions for press and press/hold actions.

Also: I replaced my Samsung S25 Ultra with this rugged model that’s half the price – and don’t regret it.

In addition, the side button above the volume buttons can be set up with double-press and long-press actions, so there are plenty of options for accessing your favorite apps and utilities through physical button actions, as anyone with experience working in the field will appreciate.

The display is not as vibrant as I am used to with AMOLED phones and watches, but it worked well for the outside conditions where I was using the tablet. The long battery life was more key for keeping me powered up while navigating the remote wilderness and if you are looking for a rugged tablet for field work then the Samsung Galaxy Tab Active5 Pro is definitely a tablet to consider.

If you’re looking for a tablet to use outside the office or in conditions where it’ll be subjected to the elements, you should consider a rugged tablet made for those use cases. The Samsung Galaxy Tab Active5 Pro is built to perform for years with very long battery life, several physical buttons to navigate the tablet, and eight years of updates. It’s reasonably priced and built to handle rough conditions.

According to recent reports, amazon is betting that many Ring customers will also want an AI-powered security drone and robot patrolling their homes or offices. But the organization’s upcoming Ring Robotic products are also certain to intensify privacy concerns previously raised around a prior Amazon attempt to popularize a flying security camera.

The Ring Rover Cam and Ring Drone Cam are expected to reach customers starting at the end of 2026 and in early 2027, respectively, according to an Amazon announcement posted on November 10. Amazon describes the devices as relying on an AI Pilot system that uses each device’s cameras along with “specialized vision models, on-device sensors and cloud processing” to initiative patrol routes while autonomously navigating around obstacles such as furniture.

Both devices also use that AI Pilot system to digitally map the floor plan of the customer’s home or business. This setup process occurs after the customer carries the Ring drone through their indoor spaces or allows the Ring Rover to do some autonomous exploration.

The AI Pilot can supposedly use that guided- or self-tour information to identify specific rooms and suggest patrol points near side doors, windows, or even sensitive locations such as a cash register in the case of a business.

However, flying and roving cameras with AI-enabled features could introduce new privacy risks for homes and businesses, on top of existing concerns involving fixed Ring cameras installed in room corners or as doorbell cameras.

Amazon’s Ring Drone appears to be a direct successor to the manufacturer’s Ring Always Home Cam that was only temporarily available for purchase by invitation as a “Day 1 Edition” product in September 2021—even having the same starting price of $250.

Sources indicate that but the Ring Drone still requires authorization from the Federal Communications Commission before going on sale. Assuming that comes through, Amazon aims to make the drone available on January 27, 2027, with customers able to register for email updates through the product page.

Onboard camera capability includes a 148-degree field of view and 360-degree rotation with a 2K video resolution. Two LED lights also activate in low-light conditions to help illuminate the scene for the drone video camera.

However, the drone is limited to just 8 minutes of flight time when operating on a “fresh, fully-charged battery under controlled conditions” according to the product description. It comes with a docking station for charging.

Another caveat in the product description is that the Ring Drone Cam may experience degraded performance when navigating in environments with reflective surfaces such as “polished marble or wet tile,” blank matte walls without any features, or transparent surfaces like frameless glass and mirrors.

According to recent reports, still, Amazon touts the drone as providing an “autonomous way to check on your home that has never existed before,” whether the customer is away or at home. The Ring Drone can be controlled directly from the Alexa Home Map interactive map that shows all of a customer’s Amazon-linked devices.

Meanwhile, Amazon has pitched the Ring Rover Cam priced at $1,000 as “an autonomous security robot designed for business.” This product is already available for preorder for those so inclined and scheduled to start shipping to customers on December 16, 2026.

The company described the Ring Rover as being inspired by customer feedback involving another invite-only beta product, the Amazon Astro robot designed for home monitoring.

According to recent reports, the Ring Rover can livestream and record in up to 4K video resolution when patrolling or while doing a 360-degree scan at a designated location. Videos triggered by doorbell rings, motion events and “Live View” events are stored in the cloud for sharing and replaying for up to 180 days.

Like the Ring Drone, the Ring Rover can automatically respond to alerts from connected Ring devices by following its preprogrammed patrol points. But the wheeled robot is only designed to operate within a single-floor, indoor environment because it lacks stair-climbing capability.

Amazon’s product description also warns that the Rover is not compatible with “curved edges, sunken areas, flooring transitions greater than 1.375 inches (3.5 centimeters), and black glossy floors.”.

To help compensate for its ground-based view, the Ring Rover comes with an automatically adjustable mast to peer over counters, shelving and other obstacles. It can supposedly cover up to 5,000 square feet (465 square meters), according to Amazon’s product description.

The Ring Rover also comes with additional security-related features such as a siren and light tower to loudly announce its presence, along with a microphone for two-way audio communication if the customer wants to address someone near the robot.

In a recent development, amazon touts the new Ring Robotics products as offering “privacy and security without compromise,” with features such as LED indicators and screen notifications informing customers when video and audio recordings are active. But Ring, as an Amazon subsidiary, has been previously implicated in multiple privacy and security scandals.

In a recent development, ring was previously charged in a 2023 Federal Trade Commission investigation with allowing employees and contractors to watch Ring video recordings of customers’ private spaces. The FTC also described Ring as having lackluster safeguards that allowed hackers to access 55,000 US customers’ accounts.

Videos taken by the fresh Ring Drone and Ring Rover will be protected with Ring’s Throw Away the Key Encryption that was introduced in September 2026, according to Amazon’s announcement. The digital rights nonprofit Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF) has described this as an improvement over Ring’s former default settings, but still well short of end-to-end encryption.

The EFF has also called out what it describes as Ring founder Jamie Siminoff’s “surveillance-first-privacy-last” approach to Ring devices, including Ring reintroducing features that allow law enforcement to request footage or live-stream access from Ring users’ home security devices.

Sources indicate that amazon’s previous attempt to launch its Ring Always Home Cam drone also led to expanded privacy concerns. Ryan Calo, a law and technology researcher at the University of Washington, previously described such a flying security camera as providing new ways to surveil others indoors, along with giving companies much greater access to potentially sensitive or identifying details of homes and businesses.

There is at the moment no mention of the fresh Ring Robotics products implementing facial recognition or similar AI-powered technologies for identifying people. But starting in December 2025, Ring has allowed owners of fixed Ring doorbell cameras to turn on a “Familiar Faces” feature that uses facial recognition technology on visitors—and that is already the subject of a class action lawsuit.

#5041. Google DeepMind just mathematically verified key parts of Signal

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (697 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

Google DeepMind just mathematically verified key parts of Signal

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (697 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Google DeepMind researchers used agentic AI to mathematically prove, or “formally verify,” a number of the Signal protocol’s key cryptographic guarantees—a landmark development for the widely used cryptography and AI itself.
  • According to recent reports, conducted as a sort of proof-of-concept project in just four weeks, the work is significant in two ways.
  • More broadly, AI-aided formal verification is having a moment, but it is unclear how practical it will be for widespread use and how effective it can be at securing large amounts of code.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google DeepMind researchers used agentic AI to mathematically prove, or “formally verify,” a number of the Signal protocol’s key cryptographic guarantees—a landmark development for the widely used cryptography and AI itself.

According to recent reports, conducted as a sort of proof-of-concept project in just four weeks, the work is significant in two ways. It serves as further independent validation of the cryptography that protects massive quantities of the world’s communications on platforms like the Signal app, Google Messages, and WhatsApp. And it demonstrates Google DeepMind’s formal verification capabilities using a newly introduced AI framework called AlphaProof Code.

More broadly, AI-aided formal verification is having a moment, but it is unclear how practical it will be for widespread use and how effective it can be at securing large amounts of code. Proponents of formal verification have long referred to it as a sort of holy grail in software security, because it uses math to check and validate that software is functioning as intended—in other words, that it doesn’t have critical vulnerabilities.

Before the AI era, it was incredibly time-consuming for people to describe the characteristics of software they wanted to prove, turn these summaries into formulas, and then develop the proof. Agentic AI can significantly cut down the time of the latter project, enabling analyses like DeepMind’s Signal evaluation. But even this analysis was limited in scope—it did not, for example, formally verify the entire Signal mobile app—and DeepMind researchers emphasize that their findings are just one milestone in a larger process.

“We are very excited by this result, but there is a long distance to go before we are able to scale this to all the software of the world, and we want to do that,” Swarat Chaudhuri, a DeepMind research scientist, tells WIRED.

The DeepMind analysis did not find any newly introduced vulnerabilities in the portions of the Signal protocol it looked at, but when the researchers used AlphaProof Code on older versions of Signal that contain known and long-fixed vulnerabilities, it correctly identified them and revealed that the protocol could not be formally verified. The researchers are releasing the specification and proof they developed for the Signal protocol analysis to aid other formal verification work.

While the speed of the project was notable, the DeepMind researchers point out that they were able to get a head start to a degree because of some past formal verification work that the Signal Foundation has conducted.

Industry observers note that “While prior formal verification focused on smaller portions of the code, Google DeepMind’s approach enables significant expansion,” Ehren Kret, Signal’s chief technology officer, notes in a statement. “As AI-driven security threats grow, rigorously verifying the Signal protocol implementation gives us even greater confidence in our code’s privacy guarantees.”.

For critical services used in high-stakes settings, it would be a dream to be able to formally verify every code base and entire software supply chains. “If you can now verify the correctness of these implementations, then you can rest easy,” indicates Pushmeet Kohli, chief scientist at Google Cloud and DeepMind’s vice president of research. “You can imagine banks, imagine all those other companies who rely on assurances and who worry about bugs who could now say, ‘I can prove these properties.’”.

The open question across the tech sector, though, is whether AI-automated formal verification can truly scale—and whether it can do so at a workable cost. DeepMind conducted the Signal analysis free of charge as a research project, and Google declined to share the cost of the analysis. The organization also declined to comment on whether it has prepares to release a commercial formal verification product or service.

Industry observers note that the researchers say that some of their crucial advancements are in developing a “human-AI collaboration process,” as Chaudhuri puts it, that allows agents to contribute and self-correct at almost every phase of the process while still seeking human input and review at key junctures. “We don’t want this sort of vibe world where AI is generating the goals and AI is generating the proofs and basically taking tests that are self-written,” Chaudhuri indicates. “There’s a middle ground.”.

This story originally appeared on wired.com.

Mendix Studio Pro contains multiple vulnerabilities in the MCP Server, that could allow an attacker with network access to interact with the server remotely or trick a user's browser into sending unauthorized requests, potentially leading to unauthorized data access, tool execution, or system compromise. Siemens has released fresh versions for the affected products and recommends to update to the latest versions.

The following versions of Siemens Mendix Studio Pro are affected:.

Product Status: known_affected.

It has been revealed that mitigationMaintain strict inbound firewall policies (such as Windows Defender Firewall) blocking external traffic on port 7782. This is already the case by default on standard Windows installations. If remote access is required, restrict traffic via a secure, authenticated channel (e.g., a VPN or SSH tunnel) rather than opening direct inbound firewall rules.

Vendor fixUpdate to V11.16.0 or later version.

#5032. Breaking: Big Walk used AI to fix a bug. Now the indie gaming world is having a reckoning.

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1457 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Big Walk used AI to fix a bug. Now the indie gaming world is having a reckoning.

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1457 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the last few years have seen significant debate over the widespread use of AI-powered tools in game development and the responsible disclosure of that usage to players.
  • This particular controversy has been brewing behind the scenes for months, as judges and jury members for the prestigious Independent Games Festival Awards discussed the glitch in private discussion groups.
  • Noting “a significant increase in the number of submitted games developer with generative AI tools,” the group of jurors called out AI’s ecological, economic, psychological, and labor harms in rejecting tools whose use, they said, is still “not a foregone conclusion in our industry.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the last few years have seen significant debate over the widespread use of AI-powered tools in game development and the responsible disclosure of that usage to players. That debate has exploded into a full-blown controversy in the indie game development space this week, as Major Walk developer House House has publicly and belatedly disclosed minimal AI use in its popular co-operative puzzle exploration game.

This particular controversy has been brewing behind the scenes for months, as judges and jury members for the prestigious Independent Games Festival Awards discussed the glitch in private discussion groups. But the debate started to break into public view on Monday when 19 members of the 50-plus-member jury released a signed statement outlining a stance “declining to vote for any game that uses generative AI in any capacity.”.

Noting “a significant increase in the number of submitted games developer with generative AI tools,” the group of jurors called out AI’s ecological, economic, psychological, and labor harms in rejecting tools whose use, they said, is still “not a foregone conclusion in our industry.”.

The jurors also urged the IGF as a whole to “adopt a strong anti-AI policy for future years that disallows games containing any AI-generated work.”.

Although the jurors’ statement didn’t name any specific games, by Tuesday morning, one critical darling in particular was increasingly being noted as a central part of the debate. In a statement provided to Aftermath (and added to the game’s FAQ page shortly thereafter), developer House House admitted publicly that “LLMs were used sparingly” near the end of Major Walk‘s development “to help work through some difficult technical challenges and bugs.”.

According to recent reports, that limited AI use—which House House indicates represents “well under 0.1% of Major Walk‘s code—stemmed in part from a thorny Unity engine bug that was slowing the game down with “infinite length” shadows during some game situations. After consulting with a Unity engineer who determined a fix “wasn’t possible,” House House stated it consulted an LLM chatbot, which suggested a possible fix that the developers “had to modify… extensively” into the 10 lines of code that ended up in the final game (At least one social media user says the bug was indeed fixable with significant human effort, though).

House House said it didn’t disclose this LLM usage for Massive Walk‘s Steam release earlier this year because Valve “does not request disclosure of code or chatbot usage.” Indeed, Valve’s AI disclosure form for developers specifically notes that it is concerned with AI-generated content, not “efficiency gains” from “modern game development environments [that] have AI powered tools built into them.”.

Industry observers note that the IGF Awards make no such distinction for AI usage, however, which led House House to mention its AI-assisted bug fix in submitting the game for awards consideration. A version of that disclosure is being made public now because “it has become a matter of public interest,” House House said.

“This is not an endorsement of, or argument for, the use of AI tools, however minimal,” House House wrote. “We have some concern that voluntary disclosures like this might contribute to the normalization of this technology, or its treatment as ‘inevitable.’ We support the work of those who are trying to limit the harm generative AI is doing to videogames and our world, and apologize that Massive Walk’s LLM usage may not meet their standards.”.

In a recent development, learning of House House’s AI disclosure was particularly painful for some IGF judges who had previously felt a special connection to Major Walk. In a blog post discussing his feelings, IGF jurist Austin Walker called the game “an achievement” that was “remarkable” and “beautiful,” featuring puzzles that “capture a range of play that is largely abandoned by the digital form.” Fellow jurist Damon Reece shared in a blog post that the game is “seriously special to me” and that it gave him “a profound and powerful emotional reaction to being in a space that felt like home.”.

But when it comes to IGF awards consideration, Walker and Reece were among those who stated that even minimal use of AI tools overrode that deep and abiding respect for the work itself.

“We have our hands on the lever here,” Reece wrote. “This is pain that has to happen [emphasis in original] to try and steer our culture away from this. We need to choose to speak loudly and clearly on this, to prioritize human creativity and labour, to tell the culture and the world that this is unacceptable to us. To do otherwise is rank cowardice.”.

This isn’t the first time AI usage has noticeably affected game award judging. Last year, the Indie Game Awards (which are completely separate from the IGF Awards) rescinded awards for Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 after the developers admitted that some in-game textures were made using AI tools (these were later patched out).

“The Indie Game Awards have a hard stance on the use of gen AI throughout the nomination process and during the ceremony itself,” they noted at the time.

According to recent reports, since House House’s public disclosure, the anti-AI contingent of IGF judges has found plenty of support from disappointed Major Walk fans and industry observers. In the last few days, the game’s Steam page has been bombed with over 400 negative reviews, though Steam’s anti-review-bomb tools seem to be limiting the impact on the game’s overall “Very Positive” reception there.

But others feel House House’s relatively minimal use of AI here is being blown out of proportion. They say it’s notable to differentiate between games that use LLMs as a last-resort technical fix, for instance, and others that lean heavily on AI to generate the bulk of their art, music, or the core of the game engine itself.

IGF judge Liz Ryerson wrote on social media that she didn’t find House House’s AI use to be personally disqualifying for the awards and that “the fact that many acted like there aren’t any levels to this and it’s all the same is bothersome to me.”.

Recent findings suggest that “To feel like someone gets punished a lot more for transparency about a smaller level of fuckup vs. just not even attempting to be honest or transparent at all is what bothers me,” she wrote.

Steam Hype staff writer and prolific Steam curator Dominic Tarason also pushed back against the idea that “House House need to be memory-holed and their work never spoken of again” as a “penalty for touching the Forbidden Device.” He mentioned he considers Substantial Walk “very mildly compromised art” that is still “absolutely, unquestionably art and very human.”.

“They spent years on that work of art,” Tarason added. “They asked a chatbot for two minutes how to fix a bug. That’s a ‘That’s lame, don’t do that again’ failing. … Some of you are acting like they’ve been convicted of high crimes against humanity, to be sealed away in the darkest oubliette until not even bones remain.”.

Sources indicate that but some have argued that using AI to fix a bug rather than hiring an expert to figure it out did make the game’s development at least a bit less human than it could have been. “House House aren’t laying off developers to replace them with Claude, and I’m sure they would be firmly against the mere thought of doing this, but we can also clearly see how their actions are part of the same problem,” AI researcher Mike Cook wrote on his blog.

Still, game developer, author, and professor Brendan Keogh wrote that he thinks “an extreme zero tolerance of any [generative AI] is ultimately counterproductive now. [There’s] a lot of anger at devs that feel deeply conflicted enough about their glorified Google search to disclose it, and [that is] encouraging those using it to actually steal labor to hide that use.”.

Sources indicate that as time goes on and AI tools are increasingly used in the building of major game engines, it may become increasingly difficult for anti-AI absolutists to avoid every game that has been touched by even a hint of LLM-generated code (if that use is even disclosed in the first place). That mentioned, many still see value in a firm and unyielding public stance against what they see as a scourge to their entire industry.

Recent findings suggest that “I think zero tolerance is a viable political position,” narrative designer and writer Hannah Nicklin wrote on social media. “You use politics against systems, for people you affect change through connection and understanding… The IGF jury statement… levels itself at a system of shared value and asks for change to enable solidarity around a position of harm reduction.”.

If you’re interested in buying a rugged tablet, you should consider the following:.

It has been revealed that pen or no pen: In many cases, having the ability to use a stylus to easily mark up drawings or photos, take notes, and navigate the user interface with gloves on is an important element of using the rugged tablet in the field. If you decide that a stylus is essential, then that will help you narrow down your choice of rugged tablet.

Sources indicate that size and weight: The environment you will be working in and the type of work you proposal to do with the tablet may help you decide how large the tablet can be for remaining productive. While a large display tablet may be great for viewing large drawings, it may also be cumbersome if you are using it while crawling into small spaces. Check out the size and weight of the tablets to see which works best for you.

Price: Rugged tablets are generally more expensive than a standard tablet with no protection from the elements. However, the price can vary quite a bit, so pick a range that works for you as you start to eliminate those tablets that are priced higher than you are willing to pay.

Industry observers note that specifications: The processor, RAM, and storage capabilities will help define the performance experience of your selected tablet. If you plan to use a rugged tablet with just one or two apps running, you may not be as concerned about the amount of RAM available. Many of these tablets support microSD expansion cards, too, so the amount of internal storage is then not as important as the amount of available RAM.

The ZDNET team chose all of the tablets included in this list based on their performance when tested in the real world. When we test tablets, we typically follow the same routine for each one to see which performs best.

Industry observers note that display: We measure the brightness level in different lighting conditions and assess color accuracy. We also compare the display’s performance with what the manufacturer promised, test the screen’s responsiveness to touch, and assess the performance of any extra features, like a manufacturer’s stylus.

Performance: For real-world performance metrics, our reviewers measure how rapidly the tablet reacts to input, assess game performance and frame rates, test how the tablet handles having multiple apps running simultaneously, measure the time it takes to launch apps, and even assess the tablet’s temperature during intensive tasks.

For audio, we look at the sound quality and overall listening experience, including audio clarity at different volumes, stereo separation of left and right audio channels, maximum volume level in various environments, and if there is perceived distortion.We picked these top rugged tablets by using them in shipyards, forests, and other outside environments with sand, dirt, rain, and other elements.For a deeper look into our testing process, check out our comprehensive tablet testing methodology.

For audio, we look at the sound quality and overall listening experience, including audio clarity at different volumes, stereo separation of left and right audio channels, maximum volume level in various environments, and if there is perceived distortion.

According to recent reports, A rugged tablet is a tablet that has been designed to withstand extreme conditions. Whether it’s severe weather, very high or very low temperatures, or drops and shocks, the extra-durable case protects the delicate internal components from damage and corrosion. Rugged tablets are best for mobile professionals who do a lot of fieldwork, like construction contractors and engineers. However, they can also apply to families with smaller children who can be more punishing with electronics.

Yes and no. Some of the higher-end cases, like those from Otterbox, are certainly designed to protect your tablet. But there are some aspects of a rugged tablet it can’t reproduce.

For example, some of the tablets in this roundup are designed to withstand severe temperatures in addition to being tougher to break when dropped. They also offer moisture and dust resistance — a must to protect your asset in an outdoor environment.

If a device is advertised as “military grade,” that doesn’t necessarily mean it was developed for military use but rather rigorously tested against MIL-STD 810 standards. This testing process runs devices through extreme conditions to simulate what soldiers may encounter during deployment or combat.

The standards compare device performance in situations where it may be violently dropped, thrown, or even exploded. They also test how devices hold up in heavy rain, high and low temperatures, coming into contact with chemicals, and resist dust and fungus infiltration.

Most commercially available “military grade” devices are tested for drops, shocks, and water resistance.

It has been revealed that on this list, the Acer Enduro T1, the Samsung Galaxy Tab Active Pro, and the Dell Latitude 7220 are all super durable and have features like gorilla glass. Plus, they are drop-tested and protected with impressive IP ratings.

In a recent development, IP rating indicates whether the device resists surface particles like dust (I) and moisture (P). It is why, when looking for a rugged tablet, you’ll want to pay attention to the device’s IP rating. In both instances, the higher the number, the better resistance it offers.

Sources indicate that rugged tablets are on the high end of most price points, so it can be tempting to get a regular, consumer-grade model and plunk it in a “rugged” case. And that will work… for a time.

Cases can only do so much to protect internal components like processors and storage drives from damage that can occur from bumps, shocks, and moisture. However, a tablet designed by the manufacturer to handle extreme conditions is much better equipped to handle just about anything you can throw at it.

From waterproofed and reinforced cases to hot-swappable batteries, a rugged tablet can be a great investment and valuable asset for mobile professionals working in all kinds of weather.

It has been revealed that getac builds their laptops for tough conditions, and their tablets are no different. ZDNET’s Matthew Miller got to test out the Getac K120 G3 and was impressed with the screen’s peak brightness of 1200 nits, which made it perfect for use in sunlight.

According to recent reports, the Oukitel RT3 Pro provides robust protection against drops, dust, and moisture without making you spend a fortune. For around $230, you’ll get an 8-inch display, up to 1TB of storage with a microSD card, and a 5150mAh battery.
