'Doomed From the Start': President Trump's Meme Coin Hits New Lows After Midterms

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (839 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Decrypt

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • President Trump's official meme coin has reached latest lows since he suffered a major blow in the U.S.
  • Over the weekend, the TRUMP coin touched $0.896, marking the lowest point the token had ever stooped.
  • In a recent development, luke Nolan, senior researcher at CoinShares, told Decrypt the midterms "added pressure to an already struggling token." Trading volume increased around the vote, and he believes some traders had bet on a Republican surprise win.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

President Trump's official meme coin has reached latest lows since he suffered a major blow in the U.S. midterm elections. The token has dropped almost 40% since election day, and analysts warn that new congressional scrutiny could push it lower.

Over the weekend, the TRUMP coin touched $0.896, marking the lowest point the token had ever stooped. It has since bumped 8%, sitting at $0.965, which is still down almost 40% from election day and 98.7% from its all-time high of $73.43, set the day after it rolled out, per Decrypt data.

In a recent development, luke Nolan, senior researcher at CoinShares, told Decrypt the midterms "added pressure to an already struggling token." Trading volume increased around the vote, and he believes some traders had bet on a Republican surprise win. He stated there was a "visible unwind" that led to a "sharp drawdown" after the election results rolled out.

It has been revealed that "Democrats take both chambers in January and plan to use their subpoena power on his crypto ventures. His net approval rating has almost never been lower," Max Shannon, senior associate at Bitwise Europe, told Decrypt. "It is still possible this continues to decline and, therefore, has a negative effect on these Trump-affiliated assets.".

Industry observers note that other Trump-linked assets have also taken a hit. Since the election, World Liberty Financial's WLFI token has dropped 7.5%, per Decrypt data, and shares of the Trump Media & Technology Group have dropped 32%.

Trump launched TRUMP on January 17, 2025, three days before his second inauguration, which Shannon described as "close to the peak of his popularity." Since then, the coin has faced significant scrutiny over how much the President and his family have profited from it. (The First Lady following suit and launching her own meme coin didn't help matters.).

According to recent reports, the president’s crypto ventures also became a sticking point for the Clarity Act, a bill that aimed to provide a formal legal structure for most cryptocurrency activity. Democrats scrutinized the Trump family's involvement in the crypto industry, which profited them more than $1 billion in a year.

A July draft would have barred public officials and employees, along with their spouses, from issuing or sponsoring digital assets while in office. That draft didn’t extend to officials’ children, including Don Jr. and Eric Trump, and the provision would have expired in January 2029.

Industry observers note that the bill failed a key Senate procedural vote in September. Patrick Witt, former executive director of the President’s Council of Advisers for Digital Assets, later remarked the “political problem of ethics really consumed everything else.”.

Industry observers note that TRUMP has "no value accrual, and it has been left in the dust of this narrative," Shannon stated. "Google Trends reveals searches for $TRUMP essentially flatlining since June 2025.".

In a recent development, nolan agreed, saying the coin’s appeal was "largely speculative," with no clear link between holding it and sharing in any underlying business success. The most it offered, he remarked, was the exclusive dinner to the top holders, which was both popular and controversial, depending on who you asked.

"In my view, that was just an attempt to prop up the token without actually creating any long-term demand for it," he stated.

Interest in these dinners has dried up too. Ahead of the third gala scheduled for the event of the month, 185 holders of the token were invited to register, but only 130 wallets showed on the final leaderboard. Those wallets held a combined $8.6 billion worth of TRUMP, according to Reuters, which is a 94% decline from the first dinner.

Then there's the "unappealing" token supply structure, Nolan said. The majority of tokens were allocated to Trump-linked entities and are being slowly unlocked, which means demand needs to keep growing to soak up newly injected supply.

"That is a difficult position for an asset whose main attraction is attention around one individual," he mentioned.

And what happens when Trump loses power? He has said he "would love" to serve a third term, but that remains unconstitutional—so the clock is ticking on his presidency.

It has been revealed that "I think overall Trump leaving office probably means the token continues its gradual decline," Nolan told Decrypt. "Any major Trump headlines probably make it experience the same dead cat bounces (sharp rallies) we have seen it have during short periods of time.".

Shannon thinks Trump doesn't even need to lose power for the token to keep going down. He said that it is "incredibly unlikely" that the token reclaims its highs, as it would require it to boost 82x, too many investors have been burned, and the majority of the supply is still to be unlocked.

"I think the meme coin was doomed from the start, and like with most meme coins, creating long-term demand is a Sisyphean task," Nolan told Decrypt.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ubuntu 27.04, Tenacious T-Rex, is set for an April 22, 2027 release. Although that seems a long way off, it’s sooner than you think. As is implied by the release number, 27.04 is not an LTS release, so it only receives support for nine months (until January 2028). The good news is that you can migrate from 27.04 to 27.10, and then to the LTS release, 28.04. The entire upgrade path ensures that you don’t have to miss a single release.

But what’s coming in Ubuntu 27.04? Given that it’s an interim release, you’re probably assuming that there’ll be nothing exciting to be found. Although there won’t be any game-changing additions, there will be plenty of refinements and bug fixes.

Also: I’ve used Ubuntu for 22 years – and 26.10 might be its best release yet.

According to recent reports, I’ve been using the daily release of Ubuntu 27.04 for a bit. Let’s take a look at what is right now expected in Tenacious T-Rex.

Recent findings suggest that this is probably the biggest addition to the next release of Ubuntu. And although you won’t find any major changes in GNOME, there are some important ones. First off, there will be editable quick settings, which allow for customizing, adding, removing, and rearranging toggles and widgets. GNOME 52 will also enjoy a revamped calendar popover, which streamlines the feature to focus primarily on events, time, and weather.

It has been revealed that also: Over Ubuntu? Fedora is the Linux distro I’d hop to next – here’s why.

There will also be several improvements to window management, such as a spatial overview and a mosaic/tiling system for auto-resizing and organizing windows, a refined full-screen Alt+Tab app switcher, which will be capable of grouping older windows by application while showing newer ones individually, and finally, the ability to remember window sizing, placement, and workspace.

In a recent development, desktop search is also getting a bit of polish by way of a redesigned popover and an improved results overlay that includes file previews, multiple actions, and search filters. And, as usual, there will be plenty of bug fixes and performance enhancements. The bump in speed is noticeable, too, in my testing.

Ubuntu 27.04 will ship with the Linux 7.6 kernel, which includes better VRAM management for gaming and expanded support for modern hardware, such as early enablement for AMD Zen 6, stable support for Intel Xe3P, mainline boot capabilities for Apple M3 Pro/Max/Ultra, and initial support for the 2026 Steam Controller.

There will also be performance gains for both the Btrfs and Ext4 file systems, which (along with the improvements in GNOME 52) will make Ubuntu 27.04 one of the best-performing releases in some time.

Also: This lightweight Linux distro revives old PCs destined for the junk pile – and it’s beautiful.

I will say this: I’ve come to count on Ubuntu’s latest releases to be an improvement over the previous iterations, and from what I’ve seen so far in my testing, 27.04 will not disappoint. It may not knock you back to prehistoric times, but Tenacious T-Rex will wow you with its performance and polished looks.

Breaking: Taiwan’s chipmaking giant TSMC to invest $1B in Anthropic, OpenAI

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (388 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Top chip manufacturer TSMC is ready to invest $1 billion in Anthropic and OpenAI.
  • In a recent development, the chipmaker’s board approved plans to invest up to $500 million in OpenAI preferred stock reserved for large investors and another $500 million to purchase Anthropic common shares at the latter’s expected IPO price, according to Reuters.
  • But analysts also warned that such circular financing among investors, suppliers, and customers has made it difficult to evaluate real market demand for AI-related hardware and services, according to the Journal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Top chip manufacturer TSMC is ready to invest $1 billion in Anthropic and OpenAI. That would give the Taiwanese chipmaker direct stakes in leading AI developers, even as its own contract chipmaking business has profited enormously from the AI data center buildout.

In a recent development, the chipmaker’s board approved plans to invest up to $500 million in OpenAI preferred stock reserved for large investors and another $500 million to purchase Anthropic common shares at the latter’s expected IPO price, according to Reuters. Such an investment may give markets “a shot of confidence as the artificial-intelligence trade indicates signs of strain,” The Wall Street Journal reported.

But analysts also warned that such circular financing among investors, suppliers, and customers has made it difficult to evaluate real market demand for AI-related hardware and services, according to the Journal.

Sources indicate that TSMC’s chip fabrication plants physically produce the vast majority of Nvidia’s chips designed for AI data center workloads and make most of Apple’s custom chips used in iPhones, Mac laptops and desktops, plus Apple’s planned AI computing server. Most of these fabs are located in Taiwan, but TSMC also operates fabs in Japan and China, and it has an expanding US manufacturing cluster in Arizona. It is also building a newly introduced fab in Germany.

Sources indicate that meanwhile, Anthropic and OpenAI are both purchasing huge quantities of AI hardware manufactured by TSMC for their data center projects. So TSMC’s revealed investment certainly seems to fit into the broader trend of circular financing that has become common during the AI boom, even as tech stocks have gyrated recently as investors have grown increasingly jittery.

Still, TSMC has plenty of money to spare on such a bet. Ongoing demand for AI-related chips has enabled the Taiwanese chipmaker to report six consecutive quarters of record profit, with the latest example being the organization earning more than $23 billion in profit during the July through September 2026 quarter, according to Reuters.

TSMC’s planned investment in Anthropic and OpenAI also pales in comparison with circular financing deals from major US tech companies. The most notable example is Nvidia, which has invested $30 billion in OpenAI and $10 billion in Anthropic so far, in addition to putting tens of billions of dollars into many other AI and robotics companies.

Morning Minute: Nvidia Beats, Board Says ‘No’ on Jensen

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Morning Minute is a daily newsletter written by Tyler Warner.
  • Recent findings suggest that six days after Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of the organization he co-founded 33 years ago, Nvidia delivered the best quarter in its history.
  • Fourth-quarter guidance came in at $130 billion against the $125.3 billion Wall Street wanted, with China assumed at zero.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Morning Minute is a daily newsletter written by Tyler Warner. The analysis and opinions expressed are his own and do not necessarily reflect those of Decrypt. And check out our daily news show 'FOMO HOUR' covering all of the top stories and market action.

🖥️ Nvidia Beats, Board Says ‘No’ on Jensen.

Recent findings suggest that six days after Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of the organization he co-founded 33 years ago, Nvidia delivered the best quarter in its history. And told him he isn’t coming back.

Fourth-quarter guidance came in at $130 billion against the $125.3 billion Wall Street wanted, with China assumed at zero.

And the CFO raised their 2028 revenue outlook to 75% year-over-year growth.

Just an absolute smash all around.

According to recent reports, then board chair Harvey Jones got on the call and remarked it plainly. “The Nvidia board does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.” The directors unanimously accepted his resignation, and Jones declined to answer anything about the circumstances or the independent investigation still running.

Huang had publicly offered to come back hours earlier, saying he would do it if directors believed it served shareholders and employees. Trump and Elon Musk both backed the idea. A petition passed 182,000 signatures including nearly 9,000 self-identified Nvidia employees. None of it moved the room.

According to recent reports, nvidia has hired Heidrick & Struggles to run the permanent search. Colette Kress stays interim CEO while remaining CFO, with Jones saying the board has “every confidence in Colette’s leadership, integrity and ability to deliver.” The board also created a National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee, chaired by director Suzanne Nora Johnson, to receive reports from the company’s national security and trade compliance teams.

And after all of that—the stock rose about 3%.

Recent findings suggest that A 6% revenue beat, guidance $5 billion above consensus, a new product cycle shipping, and the market gave it two percent. Shares sit roughly 35% below their October peak near $240. Nvidia perps on Hyperliquid were doing nearly a billion dollars of daily volume through the week, bouncing off $150 before settling near $162.

In a recent development, as for impact on the broader AI trade, Nvidia proved AI demand is not collapsing. You cannot manufacture $107.6 billion of data center revenue, and margins at 74.8% mean nobody is discounting to move product. The demand-collapse thesis died on Tuesday.

Two details do belong to the bears though. Growth is decelerating from 103% to roughly 77% once you strip the extra week out of Q4 guidance. And gross margin guides down about three points, from 74.8% to between 71% and 72%. Slowing growth plus compressing margins is how multiples come down regardless of how big the absolute numbers get.

The honest read is that the AI business is fine and the AI trade has stopped responding to it. For crypto that matters more than it should, because the correlation that dragged Bitcoin from $87,000 to the low $60s over six weeks ran through this exact trade.

Now we wait for the Fed on December 9 and insight into the 2027 rate hike cycle (or lack thereof) to determine the likely near-term fate.

Google pushes privacy angle as Gemini-powered smartglasses debut starting at $395

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1002 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Smartglasses have always faced an uphill road to acceptance.
  • These devices are a collaboration between Google, Samsung, and the aforementioned eyewear designers.
  • Warby Parker has designed three frames for Google eyewear, called Alden, Reid, and Wren (see above).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Smartglasses have always faced an uphill road to acceptance. Not only is propping a computer up on your nose an uncomfortable proposition, but the privacy aspect has been vexing people since the Google Glass days. Now, Google is ready to take another swing at “intelligent eyewear” for the Gemini era after previewing its intends a couple of times. The first glasses are up for preorder today from Gentle Monster and Warby Parker, but they’re no impulse buy.

These devices are a collaboration between Google, Samsung, and the aforementioned eyewear designers. Gentle Monster and Warby Parker have each designed a few different frames, with options for transparent and tinted lenses. Samsung is providing the computing hardware that fits inside them, and Google has the software covered.

Warby Parker has designed three frames for Google eyewear, called Alden, Reid, and Wren (see above). They are available with both standard optical and sun lenses in Pine, Saddle, and Jet Black colors at $395 and higher. Warby Parker is only selling devices in the US. Gentle Monster has gone a bit further with six styles, but Google hasn’t told us any names for those yet. They come in dark red, pink, gray, and yellow colors and are available with clear, tinted, blue, or brown lenses. The Gentle Monster styles start a little higher at $449, and they will be available in the US and South Korea.

Google notes the frames all weigh about 41 grams, which is not terrible but is definitely near the top for glasses generally. They will, naturally, weigh much more when you account for lenses. That will also determine the final pricing. So far, we only have the starting prices for these devices, including non-prescription lenses.

According to recent reports, the setup here is similar to the Ray-Ban Meta glasses we’ve seen for a few years. There are no screens in the lenses, but you can interact with the AI system via voice or by activating the integrated camera. The experience should be similar to using Gemini Live on your phone, but it will be a lot easier to fire up the AI. You can say “Hey Gemini” or tap a touch-sensitive area of the frame to start interacting with the robot.

Credit: Gentle Monster Credit: Gentle Monster.

According to recent reports, since this is the same chatbot that operates across the Google ecosystem, it has access to your data and preferences. You can ask questions and get personalized answers, have Google Maps guide you by voice, or just talk with the AI to kill time. The glasses use custom open-ear speakers to limit distractions for those around you. Google notes the directional microphones should not pick up speech from other people, either.

In a recent development, adding the camera feed is where things get interesting. When the AI can see what you see, it has the potential to do more work on your behalf. Google suggests asking Gemini for recommendations when looking at a bookshelf or glancing at an event poster to have the AI add it to your calendar. The glasses will also support Gemini Guided Vision, which provides conversational audio descriptions for people who are visually impaired.

The utility of these devices hinges on Gemini. I would be remiss not to point out that Gemini, like all AI systems, is not infallible. In fact, it can be frustratingly fallible at times. The chatbot still regularly screws up simple things like adding calendar appointments or identifying objects in an image in my testing, and when you don’t have a screen to verify the AI’s output, it may be harder to trust it. These devices will really only make sense if you can rely on Gemini to do things right, and that’s still not a guarantee.

All the Gemini-powered glasses from Gentle Monster and Warby Parker feature a 12 MP wide-angle camera capable of shooting photos and video. Google says it has implemented a number of features and limitations to ensure people don’t do creepy things with its intelligent eyewear, and that it doesn’t do creepy things to you—Google claims its approach respects privacy on “both sides of the lens.”.

Recent findings suggest that for starters, there’s a recording light that is on whenever the camera is active. Like the Meta glasses, Google’s eyewear will detect if the light has been covered up or modified in any way that would prevent it from illuminating. In that event, the glasses will refuse to activate the camera. All Google-powered glasses will have a physical off switch, too.

Credit: Warby Parker Credit: Warby Parker.

Sources indicate that on the user privacy side, Google says it will not save any images or videos captured by the glasses in your Gemini history. Additionally, none of that data will be used for training AI models or targeting ads. Your voice interactions with Gemini via the glasses are, as with all other Gemini endpoints, not guaranteed the same level of protection. You can delete your chats from the Gemini history, though.

Data on the glasses is encrypted, and it remains that way during transit to the cloud. However, it’s not encrypted on Google’s servers. The organization does note that it’s working to bring Private AI Compute to glasses, which will isolate data during processing so not even Google can access it.

Credit: Gentle Monster Credit: Gentle Monster.

Sources indicate that anyone looking to get Gemini on their face and test Google’s privacy promise can preorder the glasses from the Gentle Monster and Warby Parker websites. Devices should ship and appear on store shelves on December 10. Importantly, support for these devices is a bit narrow at launch. They will work with all iPhones from the 13 Pro onward. On the Android side, you’ll need a Pixel 7 or newer or a Samsung Galaxy S or Z series device running One UI 9 or later. If you’ve got a cheaper Samsung Galaxy or a device from another OEM, you’re out of luck at the moment.

Hundreds of readers bought these 10 most popular robot vacuums in 2026

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As a smart home reviewer, I’m especially fond of robot vacuums.
  • We test dozens of robot vacuums each year at ZDNET, both in our lab and at home.
  • Our team also compiles data on the top-selling robot vacuums across various retailers each year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As a smart home reviewer, I’m especially fond of robot vacuums. I enjoy unboxing, setting up, and testing these devices, and I love seeing newly introduced technologies emerge each year. Even when robot vacuums look similar, each one is actually quite different, which means I’m constantly learning new things about these devices.

We test dozens of robot vacuums each year at ZDNET, both in our lab and at home. As a result, I’m always writing reviews of different models and updating our choices to reflect the best units you can buy.

Also: Best early Black Friday deals.

Our team also compiles data on the top-selling robot vacuums across various retailers each year. The following are listed in order of units sold, based on the links clicked from ZDNET stories thus far in 2026. (A note: Your privacy is protected — we only have access to aggregate data from our user base, and there is no way for us to identify individual people’s purchases.).

Recent findings suggest that the Roborock Saros 10R was ZDNET’s pick for the best robot vacuum and mop of 2025, and the winner of a ZDNET Editors’ Choice award. It features industry-leading 22,000Pa of suction and a slim 3.14-inch-tall design that allows it to navigate under low furniture. It also has Roborock’s VertiBeam Lateral Obstacle Avoidance technology to prevent it from getting entangled in cords and other small obstacles on your floors.

The Ecovacs Deebot X11 OmniCyclone is a powerful robot vacuum with a superb self-emptying mechanism and a unique charging feature. The dock uses a dust canister instead of a replaceable dust bag, so you don’t have to worry about buying replacements every few months. The robot itself has the longest battery life I’ve tested, thanks to GaN charging. Every time the robot goes to the dock to auto-empty or wash its mop, the dock uses fast charging to top off the battery, extending its life.

In a recent development, the Roborock Q7 M5+ is a surprisingly effective budget-friendly robot vacuum. It can handle pet hair in your home with its powerful 10,000Pa of suction for only $200 (for a limited time). This is a budget-friendly robot that doesn’t promise more than it can deliver. As a result, you can rest assured that it will complete the basics of vacuuming and light mopping done well.

Recent findings suggest that the Mova P50 Pro Ultra is the top performer against pet hair out of all the robot vacuums I’ve tried — and I’ll happily die on this hill. It has an anti-tangle CleanChop brush and, while most robots claim to have anti-tangle brushes, this one actually cuts hair as it rolls, so it never tangles. This robot reliably keeps my floors hair-free, even with a medium-length-haired dog who sheds like crazy.

To boot, the Mova P50 Pro Ultra also has a self-washing mop and auto-emptying dustbin for hands-free cleaning.

The Eufy Omni S1 Pro is one of the best robot vacuum and mop combos I’ve ever tested. As a reviewer, I get a lot of these devices and often don’t have room to keep them — but the S1 Pro is the one I’ve kept the longest in my home. It features precise cleaning and obstacle avoidance, and its mop roller is the best one I’ve seen in a robot of this type.

Recent findings suggest that the successor to the S1 Pro is now available and even more impressive. You can read my experience with the Eufy Omni S2 here.

One of the top performers among affordable robot vacuums, I wasn’t surprised to see the 3i G10+ on the list of most purchased models. Upcoming units are no longer available for purchase on Amazon, though you can find it used for about $100. Since the G10+ doesn’t have a self-emptying dustbin, it features a dustbin compression system that lets you go up to 60 days before emptying — completely bag-free.

According to recent reports, the mop roller doesn't only mop with clean water, but it also extends along the edge of a wall or furniture to clean. / Maria Diaz/ZDNET.

The Ecovacs X8 Pro Omni is the recipient of the ZDNET Lab Award for best pickup performance in a robot vacuum, which means it was the most effective at vacuuming debris in our lab tests. With 18,000Pa of suction and effective navigation, this robot cleans every inch of my floors. I love the roller mop on it, which extends to clean along wall edges, and always mops with clean water.

Recent findings suggest that the Mova Mobius 60 features interchangeable mop pads that automatically swap based on the area or mess the robot is cleaning. If it’s going to clean the kitchen, the Mobius 60 goes back to the dock to “grab” the ThermoHold Mop that is good for oily messes. When it needs to clean hardwood and delicate surfaces, it uses the Plush Mop. The HyperClean Mop is for all areas, comprised of composite fibers.

The RV20 Max is a beginner-friendly robot vacuum for people who don’t like the bulky base stations taking up space at home. Priced at $199, the RV20 Max works surprisingly well, with 5,300Pa of suction power and navigation that doesn’t rely on bump-and-run. The trade-off is that this robot doesn’t have the best obstacle-avoidance capabilities, so it may get stuck on cables and small items.

Unfortunately, this product is being discontinued, so it’s out of stock at Amazon at this point.

The Eufy C10 is a super-slim robot vacuum that is only 2.85 inches tall, perfect for fitting under low-clearance furniture. Even at this low profile, the C10 features LiDAR navigation and smart mapping. You can also go up to 8 weeks without worrying about replacing the dust bag at the dock. As a robot vacuum only, the Eufy C10 is best for mostly carpeted homes or those where you prefer to do your own mopping.

Lucky Trader Banks 66,000% Profit on GTA 6 Meme Coin Ticker Confusion

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • One lucky meme coin trader made bank as Grand Theft Auto 6 launched worldwide, turning $300 into over $200,000 after early footage of the game sent degens flocking from one unofficial token to another.
  • The trader bought $307 worth of the DCTY token shortly after it launched in October and has sold their bag for $202,278, according to DEX Screener, a profit of almost 66,000%.
  • Early indications had pointed to GTA 6 featuring an in-game meme coin—with, it's worth stressing, no actual blockchain element—called "DacityCoin," which appeared in the official launch trailer on a plane with a wing walker setting off a smoke bomb on top of it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One lucky meme coin trader made bank as Grand Theft Auto 6 launched worldwide, turning $300 into over $200,000 after early footage of the game sent degens flocking from one unofficial token to another.

The trader bought $307 worth of the DCTY token shortly after it launched in October and has sold their bag for $202,278, according to DEX Screener, a profit of almost 66,000%.

Early indications had pointed to GTA 6 featuring an in-game meme coin—with, it's worth stressing, no actual blockchain element—called "DacityCoin," which appeared in the official launch trailer on a plane with a wing walker setting off a smoke bomb on top of it.

It was later linked to leaked gameplay of an mission which appeared to show game protagonist Lucia parachuting as a stunt to attract investment to DacityCoin.

It has been revealed that amid this hype, per DEX Screener, a real-world and unofficial DacityCoin debuted using the Solana launchpad Pump.fun. It first peaked at a $4.95 million market capitalization, following the launch trailer's release, before tanking 93% to $343,620 as hype faded.

In a recent development, with GTA 6 set to launch within a matter of hours of publication, the token drew renewed attention, propelling it to a newly introduced all-time high of $10.8 million Wednesday. Unfortunately for investors, GTA 6's staggered global release means that some gamers are already playing it—and footage started to spread which suggested the Solana token's ticker was wrong.

The result was a rollercoaster of volatility, with the DacityCoin token now sitting at a market cap of around $800,000.

Gameplay footage from Brazilian streamer Combo Infinito suggests that the in-game token is called DacityCoin, with the ticker DCTY.

https://t.co/kgefwOzGCH pic.twitter.com/LEDrcP7gve.

— Dusty (@guidustyy) November 18, 2026.

That propelled another Solana token with a seemingly accurate name and ticker sprang into action. DCTY's previous all-time high market cap was just $54,000 before the ticker was revealed, and it set a new high of over $12 million after footage of the game appeared to confirm that its ticker matched the in-game token. It is now trading at a market cap of around $10 million.

Recent findings suggest that the game itself appears to be somewhat inconsistent in its naming of the in-game token. During the trailer, it appeared to be spelled "DacityCoin" as one word, however, the subtitles in the leak show it spelled as "Dacity coin," two words. Similarly, the company behind the in-game token is AudaCity, but leaks show three different spellings: Auda City, AudaCity, and Auda-City.

It is worth stressing: Rockstar has not explicitly confirmed that a meme coin will be featured in-game, and any real-world token has no official links to GTA 6 or its creators. Footage is still being released, and absolute confirmation of the in-game token's involvement is still being established.

In a recent development, those still holding the now-tanking DacityCoin are hoping things will turn around. Mike Lerro, the community takeover lead for DacityCoin, shrugged off any chance that the unofficial token's name and ticker are wrong.

According to recent reports, "No, bro. DacityCoin and AudaCity are in the game. Yes or no?" When Decrypt suggested the ticker might be wrong, he replied, "It doesn't matter… Okay and ? The person who creates it will dump on you then it goes to zero. Who's gonna [do the community takeover]? No one.".

"DACITYCOIN AND AUDACITY ARE IN THE GAME," Lerro wrote in the meme coin's Telegram. "NOTHING ELSE MATTERS.".

"It's so crazy, it'll correct itself," Lerro mentioned in an emergency Telegram group chat call. "I hope so," an investor replied.

Tech Report: What are the best ‘budget premium’ laptops of 2026? It comes down to these 3

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1435 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Zdnet

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that boring colors, dingy displays, and clunky forms — that’s what $699 on a Windows PC used to get you.
  • Also: MacBook Neo to get its most-requested upgrade.
  • We’re talking OLED displays, ultralight builds, premium touchpads and keyboards, and most importantly, bold colors that go beyond bland, corporate gray.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that boring colors, dingy displays, and clunky forms — that’s what $699 on a Windows PC used to get you. All that changed with the MacBook Neo, however. Apple’s “budget premium” laptop shook up the market, forcing manufacturers to respond with better laptops in the sub-$1,000 price point.

Also: MacBook Neo to get its most-requested upgrade.

We’re talking OLED displays, ultralight builds, premium touchpads and keyboards, and most importantly, bold colors that go beyond bland, corporate gray. With all the major PC brands releasing their own models, there are plenty of options in the budget range, and as memory costs continue to skyrocket, the timing couldn’t be better.

Industry observers note that but how do they perform? Well, they’re certainly running lighter hardware, but if you’re aware of their limitations, this may not be a bad thing. For students and kids, for example, they’re solid contenders for surfing the web, running Office 365, and working out of Google Docs. Ultimately, these laptops offer a ton of bang for their buck. Here are the top three I recommend.

Sources indicate that HP’s 2026 OmniBook 5 is a solid budget premium laptop with a lightweight, lovely build and a very attractive $649 starting price. Available in metallic pink, blue, green, and silver, it’s designed specifically to counter the MacBook Neo’s trade-offs in a thin, lightweight chassis and gorgeous OLED touchscreen display.

Recent findings suggest that at 2.56 pounds, it’s lighter and thinner than the Neo, at just 11.7mm thick when closed. It’s not a convertible, but the screen does lay completely flat, and HP’s hinge construction is solid, with almost no wobble while typing. The laptop’s physical build doesn’t feel cheap, but there is a small amount of flex and bend, particularly on the bottom plate.

Also: I went hands-on with IFA’s top MacBook Neo competitors.

The 14-inch, 2K touchscreen OLED display is the first thing you notice, and the standout feature by far. For a $649 laptop, it offers vivid contrast and good color separation, but it’s a rather glossy display, so you’ll probably find yourself repositioning it as I did during my testing.

The OmniBook 5 also addresses two other of the Neo’s biggest drawbacks: the lack of an HDMI port and keyboard backlighting, both of which are standard. It runs the Intel Core 5 320 processor, a battery-efficient chip that gives the laptop exceptional runtime — easily 10 hours of consistent use — sufficient for long days on campus if you forget your charger.

The $649 starting configuration comes with modest hardware: 8GB of memory and a 256GB SSD. That amount of memory all but relegates the laptop to everyday basic tasks like checking email, using Microsoft 365 apps, surfing the web, or writing papers. For students, kids, and teens looking for a laptop for school, that’s the name of the game. But if you’re a professional looking for more processing power, you may need to keep looking.

You can opt for 16GB of memory on the OmniBook 5, but it’ll bring the price up to $899, which just isn’t as competitive. Still, even though Windows 11 performs a little better on 8GB of RAM these days, I wouldn’t recommend opting for that amount of onboard memory and storage unless you’re confident these everyday tasks meet your expected use case.

It has been revealed that as mentioned above, students, kids, and teens will gravitate toward the OmniBook’s cool colors and lightweight design. Opting for 16GB will bring the price up, but it’ll also make it a much more well-rounded laptop, opening up use cases in photo and video editing, even gaming.

Dell’s 14S is particularly well-suited for students with Dell’s competitive student pricing blueprint. The 14S has the same Intel Core 5 320 processor as the HP OmniBook 5, but it also offers more configurations that, when paired with the student discount, don’t amount to a whole lot more cash. For example, you can get the 8GB model with 512GB of storage for $649, $100 off the regular price — a better deal than the OmniBook 5.

In a recent development, the Dell 14S also has one fantastic battery — lasting over 10 hours in my testing. For students who need something for the entire day on campus, the 14S delivers. It feels a whole lot like its premium cousin, the XPS 13, a fantastic laptop released earlier this year that received ZDNET’s Editors’ Choice award for its premium build and bang-for-buck. The 14S draws on that laptop’s premium construction and solid build.

Also: Dell 14S first look: Taking on MacBook Neo… again.

It has the same port setup as the OmniBook 5: an HDMI, two USB-Cs, and an audio jack. In terms of the keyboard and trackpad, I found the 14S to have a very “hard” click that’s relatively loud, which might be noticeable in a quiet classroom.

The 14S has the same considerations as the OmniBook, given its modest hardware. In my testing of the 14S with 8GB of RAM, for example, I found performance to be fine for everyday tasks, but there were inherent limits to processing power once a certain number of tabs were open in the browser or several apps were open at once.

According to recent reports, the 14S also comes with a non-touch FHD+ (1920×1200) IPS display that’s not as vivid as the OmniBook 5’s OLED or the MacBook Neo’s Liquid Retina. It also doesn’t come with a keyboard backlight standard, a feature the OmniBook 5 flaunts. However, I will say it’s brighter than both of the other two displays at 400 nits, and goes up to a 120Hz refresh rate.

According to recent reports, also, this laptop does have several configurations available, but the model with 16GB of RAM is priced at $1,199, much higher than the $899 OmniBook 5 with 16GB. The build quality is nice, but once you cross the $1,000 threshold, you’re opening yourself up to comparisons with Windows PCs with much more powerful specs.

Students should consider the Dell 14S first and foremost, since the education discount makes higher configurations especially compelling. For everyday users who work out of the browser and stay within the typical lineup of Microsoft productivity apps, performance is sufficiently snappy, as long as you’re using it for these kinds of tasks.

Sources indicate that the MacBook Neo started this whole conversation, bringing a gorgeous Liquid Retina display, Apple’s signature quality touchpad and keyboard, and exciting colors. Even better, it’s got great battery life thanks to Apple’s A18 Pro chip, and is as portable as you can ask for in a 13-inch model. The Neo succeeded because it did much of what its older siblings can do in MacOS — all the iPhone integrations like FaceTime, Messages, and iPhone Mirroring, with support for one external display up to 4K at 60Hz via USB-C.

Recent findings suggest that the trade-offs come in performance and build, but Apple’s choices here are smart. It foregoes keyboard backlighting, but as a work or school device, it’s not a huge deal. It skips the haptic touchpad, but Apple already makes a good mechanical one. The A18 Pro chip scales back multi-core power, but single-core performance (for the stuff you’re actually doing on the Neo) is great.

Also: My biggest concern with Apple’s near-perfect budget laptop.

All of this for $699 (or $599 with student pricing), earning ZDNET’s Editors’ Choice award for being the complete package laptop for an unheard-of price (it was $599 when it debuted, before a subsequent price hike).

In a recent development, unlike the other two laptops on this list, the MacBook Neo is locked into two configurations, each featuring 8GB of unified memory. Granted, 8GB on MacOS goes a lot further than on Windows 11, but still, you’re looking at either 256GB or 512GB of local storage, the former of which is too limiting in my opinion.

As Apple’s first and only device targeting the budget laptop market, the MacBook Neo is also a first-generation product that will undoubtedly have some build and performance improvements in its upcoming generation. As it stands, it’s unupgradeable and locked into a modest hardware configuration. How many years into the future it will continue to serve you is an open question.

The MacBook Neo serves as an excellent entry point into Apple’s ecosystem, especially as MacBook Pros continue to get more and more expensive. For anyone with an iPhone, it’s an easy companion device. The Neo is easily a main driver for students and pros alike, with excellent single-core performance and the versatility to tackle most tasks.

#5014. Google faces calls for AI moratoriums in schools after Gemini pilot backlash

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1777 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

Google faces calls for AI moratoriums in schools after Gemini pilot backlash

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1777 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • CHICAGO—Families joined protests in seven cities nationwide on Wednesday, rallying against what they see as Google’s bid to entrench its AI models in schools, turn kids of all ages into Gemini guinea pigs, and hook them on AI.
  • Industry observers note that the backlash follows a Google statement last week, confirming that there will be no way for students to use Google Search without AI.
  • In a recent development, in Chicago, many families highlighted up to protest Google, despite cold, rainy weather.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

CHICAGO—Families joined protests in seven cities nationwide on Wednesday, rallying against what they see as Google’s bid to entrench its AI models in schools, turn kids of all ages into Gemini guinea pigs, and hook them on AI.

Industry observers note that the backlash follows a Google statement last week, confirming that there will be no way for students to use Google Search without AI. While Google claimed it was giving schools “more choice, not less”—by turning off Search, Gemini, and Gemini Notebook by default—it would not provide an option that allowed Search without AI. For students, the only way to avoid interacting with AI was to remember to add “-ai” to every query, parents worried.

In a recent development, in Chicago, many families highlighted up to protest Google, despite cold, rainy weather. Waving signs, dozens of protesters marched up to Google’s downtown office as workers seemed to be leaving for the day, shouting chants like “Hey Google, nice try, we don’t want your Gemini” and “Hey, Google, leave our kids alone!”.

Called to action by a nonprofit grassroots advocacy group, the Illinois Families for Public Schools (ILFPS), some parents and students had previously won a major AI fight. In August, the group pressured Chicago Public Schools (CPS) to pull out of a Gemini pilot that would have roped in all high school students districtwide—without consulting parents. And now, ILFPS is demanding a moratorium on AI until risks to students are better understood and CPS can draft a policy to protect students from potential learning setbacks or more harmful outcomes from engaging Google’s AI bots. If the group wins, it will join cities like Los Angeles and Latest York City in cautiously banning AI in schools.

Sources indicate that most alarming to parents, Google now faces a lawsuit from a 13-year-old student in Durham, North Carolina named “Emma Doe.” As Emma has alleged, she was a happy, well-adjusted, straight-A student when she started using Gemini on her school-issued Chromebook. Emma’s parents had no idea she was using Gemini, as the lawsuit alleged that Google “deliberately” kept them in the dark while driving Emma into so-called “AI psychosis.” Over time, normal school-related interactions with the chatbot led to more intense chats, and ultimately the chatbot allegedly coached Emma to initiative her own suicide and funeral. The school warned her parents and averted the danger after an internal system flagged a chat labeled “Funeral,” but Emma’s story stoked fears of parents joining protests not just in Durham, but also in Boston; Boulder, Colorado; Chicago; Los Angeles; Upcoming York City; and Portland, Oregon.

Emma’s lawsuit accuses Google of exploiting its dominant position in education technology and “sneaking” Gemini into Chromebooks, while falsely marketing them as safe.

Recent findings suggest that “As a direct consequence of Google’s choices, Emma was baited by its defectively designed products into repeated, unmonitored, sycophantic AI chatbot interactions on her school Chromebook without her parents ever knowing. And, but for a fortunate turn of events, Google’s AI may well have manipulated Emma into taking her own life,” the lawsuit alleged. “Google must be held to account for treating the lives of children as disposable in service of its bottom line.”.

Recent findings suggest that google has promised to “continue to engage deeply with educators to ensure we are giving schools more choice, more controls, and improved Search for learning.” However, Google’s statements so far attempting to address parents’ concerns focus exclusively on documented harms to learning. On that front, Google claims that it’s solving the problem of AI eroding students’ critical thinking skills by launching yet another pilot for students. In this pilot, students using AI Mode and AI Overviews will be offered a “step-by-step guided learning through problems, so that students don’t get quick answers to schoolwork,” Google mentioned.

Cassie Creswell, executive director of ILFPS, told Ars that she’s been an advocate monitoring edtech issues for more than a decade. And even she was blindsided by Google’s AI moves.

Recent findings suggest that “I am aware of AI Overviews when you search, which have a whole slew of problems, but I did not know that you really actually just have an interface where you can interact with Gemini in the chatbot way on everyone’s Chromebook still in Chicago public schools,” Creswell said. “And that’s so disturbing.”.

Recent findings suggest that she acknowledged that kids encounter AI on their phones and shared that her daughter stated her friends like using ChatGPT better than Gemini. But she said that the fact that some kids use AI on personal devices doesn’t mean that schools should be encouraging adoption at young ages when kids’ brains are still developing, and risks remain largely unknown.

“There’s all kinds of dangerous things out in the world, but we don’t have our school district handing it to kids at their desk,” Creswell stated.

Meanwhile, schools seem to be part of the transparency problem.

Recent findings suggest that creswell noted that at the moment, the Chicago school district “is telling us their official line is that kids don’t have access to generative AI tools and that we don’t need a district-level policy on generative AI because they have guidebooks.” However, she’s reviewed Google’s CPS contracts, and they suggest that kids are interacting with generative AI and frontier models. The ongoing confusion has led parents to demand “a real policy” that the CPS “board votes on and that has the input of teachers, parents, students, and experts who are not being funded by the tech industry.”.

Creswell told Ars that parents are particularly upset that Google is not transparent about how it processes and uses student data. She’s exhaustively researched Google contracts through Freedom of Information Act requests and told Ars that dozens of agreements she reviewed offer no indication of how CPS partners like Google—as well as Anthropic and OpenAI—are handling student data. Although she understands that “it’s probably just an honest statement of fact” that Google has built AI inextricably into Search, parents have a right to know how their children’s data is ingested into Google’s models, she said.

“Any sort of transparency on what is actually happening in terms of the data that they collect and what they do with it, that is absolutely missing,” Creswell said. And “it’s very unclear what data is being saved.”.

To Creswell and other advocates, it seems likely that kids’ data is collected no matter what, since “even if you do ‘-AI,’ and you don’t get a text summary, your search data and what’s being returned is all basically inside the generative AI model.” Although Illinois law only allows commercial use of de-identified data, parents think Google should clearly explain what steps it takes to ensure data can’t be recombined to re-identify kids.

Ars reached out to Google to see if the company could clarify if Creswell’s read is accurate or if there’s any meaningful distinction between adding “-AI” to an individual query versus building a button that would automatically add “-AI” to every query. Google did not clarify, instead emphasizing that schools will control whether students can access the Gemini app, Gemini Notebook, and Search, with options to toggle each off individually, but no option to use Search without AI.

It has been revealed that emma Doe’s lawsuit alleged that Google has taken advantage of a dominant position it has held in schools since 2007 to push AI on kids and seize their data without meaningfully protecting them from the worst potential harms of its chatbot’s sycophantic design. In Chicago, CPS signed a contract with Google in 2020, “long before Gemini was rolled out,” Creswell found. Over the next two extensions of that contract, no updates were introduced to protect students’ privacy as AI advanced.

Sources indicate that presently, that policy specifies that “we receive customer data through the Core Services and process it according to the school’s (the customer’s) instructions. This customer data includes anything submitted, stored, sent, or received through Core Services by you or your school.” Google collects that data on that activity, as well as account information “like name, email address and password” and location information, the policy said.

Sources indicate that the policy didn’t discuss Gemini but noted that data from using core services helps maintain services, improve personalization, and increase security. And “the data we collect in the Additional Services is used across our services to deliver, maintain, and improve our services; develop new services; provide personalized services; measure performance; communicate with you; and protect Google, our people, and the public.”.

To parents, the policy provides no reassurance that their kids’ data isn’t part of Google’s blueprint to dominate the AI industry.

“We should not have any child data being collected in a school setting being used for commercial purposes,” Creswell mentioned.

Parents’ privacy concerns go beyond Google, Creswell noted. But since Google has “captured so much of the education space and so much of the education experience,” parents are focusing their energy on interrogating those AI systems in schools early on.

It has been revealed that in Chicago, a recently re-elected CPS school board member, Karen Zaccor, is pushing for an AI moratorium in schools after talking with city and community colleges about an allegedly noticeable decline in reading, math, and writing skills from students graduating from CPS schools. In Emma’s case, Google allegedly suppressed chat logs, and the school withheld safety logs, frustrating parents who already viewed AI as more harmful than beneficial in education.

Recent findings suggest that at the Google protest Wednesday, parents waved signs that threatened to eject Google from schools, with slogans like “No Google + No AI = Win/Win.” Many kids used favorite cartoon characters from reveals like Beavis and Butthead and South Park to slam Google’s seemingly cynical approach to introducing AI in schools. One young girl wearing pink rain boots held up a cardboard sign, declaring in colorful markers, “I like to read!!”.

At its peak, about 60 people stood outside Google’s downtown Chicago office, enduring the rain and listening to teachers and students who oppose reckless AI adoption.

One particularly moving speech came from a CPS student, Reese Mackey, who spoke for students. She challenged Google to more carefully weigh the long-term harms of aggressively pushing AI onto students by claiming they’ll be left behind and struggle to find jobs without AI skills. Creswell told Ars the opposite seems true, as Emma Doe’s lawsuit pointed to research branding Gemini as “the most dangerous marketed for use by youth” and “confirming the existence of AI-induced psychosis.”.

According to recent reports, “What about the future of our youth?” Mackey mentioned. “What about the future of our minds?”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google’s upcoming Fitbit Air is made for those of us who want to dip into fitness and health tracking, but prefer a more discreet alternative to a bulky smartwatch. It’s thin, light, and the screenless design means you’re not bothered by notifications throughout the day.

Also: Google’s Fitbit Air is a $99 screenless wearable that I can actually take seriously.

In a recent development, it’s especially good for first-time consumers curious about step counting and sleep tracking, thanks to its affordable $99 price tag. And what better time to commit to your goals than the holiday season? If you’re planning to purchase a Fitbit Air or already have one, there are a few easy ways to maximize your experience. Here are my five suggestions:.

Industry observers note that the Fitbit Air isn’t medical-grade equipment, but it can alert you if it detects irregular patterns in your heart rate. Google sends you a notification on your phone if it detects that it’s high or low while you are inactive for at least 10 minutes. However, these alerts aren’t turned on by default. You need to go to the Google Health app and follow these steps:.

Industry observers note that by default, Google calculates a custom high and low heart rate threshold based on your age and typical resting heart rate. For me, the High threshold is set to 120 beats per minute, whereas the Low threshold is set to 49 beats per minute. You can change these if you want, but I’ve left them at default.

In a recent development, like heart rate warnings, the Fitbit Air can alert you about irregular heart rhythm, but it isn’t turned on by default. You need to set it up by following these steps:.

According to recent reports, it must be noted that this feature doesn’t check for heart attacks or strokes. Google also makes it very clear that you can have AFib without receiving a notification, and some people with AFib don’t have any symptoms.

It has been revealed that during Setup, the Google Health app nudges you to choose a wrist for your Fitbit Air. For accurate step tracking, it is recommended that you wear it on your non-dominant hand because the dominant hand is used much more throughout the day, even when you’re not actively moving. This could lead to inaccurate readings. However, there are times when you might want to wear it on the dominant hand.

Also: I compared the best smartwatches by Google and Samsung – here’s how Pixel wins out.

In a recent development, for example, I’m right-handed, but I wear an analog watch on my left hand. So, there’s no space for the Fitbit Air on my left hand. Sorry, Fitbit, but the watch takes precedence. If you’re like me, you’ll need to upgrade the Wrist preference under settings to make sure your device doesn’t register every hand movement as a step. To do this, you need to:.

Changing this setting will allow the algorithms to navigate through daily movements and register actual steps more accurately.

The Google Health app indicates glanceable insights at the top of the home page, called the dashboard. By default, you’ll see stats like steps, cardio load and more located in a circular progress graph and multiple tiles. You can scroll horizontally to access more tiles. However, they might not be in the sequence you want.

For instance, I want to see my sleep insights, steps, vitals, and heart rate whenever I open the app. I don’t care about stats like Hourly activity or Hydration etc. Thankfully, Google allows you to customize this dashboard to your preference. All you need to do is:.

Google introduced an all-new AI Coach with its latest wearables. It can help make sense of your raw data, suggest workouts according to your goals, log food and answer questions regarding your fitness levels.

I’ve asked the AI coach for help in planning my workout routine, understanding my vitals, and getting recovery advice. While it can be helpful, you shouldn’t trust everything it reports. The AI Coach hallucinates pretty often. It can misreport your workout data or misunderstand goals. Like any form of AI, stay skeptical and fact check its findings.

According to recent reports, also: Are AI health coach subscriptions a scam? My verdict after testing Fitbit’s for a month.

It has been revealed that for example, in her review of the Fitbit, ZDNET’s Nina Raemont noted, “One night it [the AI Coach] mentioned a 52-minute elliptical session I had done that morning. But I didn’t exercise that day.”.

If any presented data or facts look off to you, a Google spokesperson recommended asking the Coach, “Are you sure?” or asking where the Coach got the data. This makes the Coach redo its work. I tried doing this, and it worked sometimes (but not always). I’d recommend you don’t rely on the AI Coach for everything, as it can make mistakes.

#5010. Breaking: HP OmniBook 5 review: Delivering more (and less) than the Macbook Neo

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1092 w)
📖 Baca
Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Zdnet ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: HP OmniBook 5 review: Delivering more (and less) than the Macbook Neo

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1092 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Zdnet

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that after the MacBook Neo permanently altered perceptions of what you can expect from a budget laptop, Windows PCs have been responding in turn with their own fleet of “budget premium” laptops at competitive prices.
  • Also: MacBook Neo production to double in 2027 – and get its most-requested upgrade.
  • It has been revealed that at this price point, though, it all comes down to trade-offs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that after the MacBook Neo permanently altered perceptions of what you can expect from a budget laptop, Windows PCs have been responding in turn with their own fleet of “budget premium” laptops at competitive prices. HP’s OmniBook 5 is one such laptop, with a vibrant OLED display, colorful build, and all-day battery starting at $649.

Also: MacBook Neo production to double in 2027 – and get its most-requested upgrade.

It has been revealed that at this price point, though, it all comes down to trade-offs. For the Neo, you lose out on keyboard backlighting, flexible configurations (it’s locked at 8GB of memory), and a lack of ports — all things the OmniBook 5 addresses.

HP broke up its typical lineup of gray, corporate laptops this year with more attractive colors and builds, particularly the OmniBook X Flip 14, with a unique espresso color that caught my eye. The OmniBook 5, however, takes a bubblier approach in metallic pastel pink, blue, green, and silver colorways and a thin, lightweight chassis.

Sources indicate that at 2.56 pounds, it’s lighter than the Neo and thinner as well (as evidenced by the full-screen side-by-side image comparison on HP’s site) at just 11.7mm thick when closed. It’s not a convertible, but the screen does lay completely flat, and HP’s hinge construction is solid, with almost no wobble while typing. The laptop’s physical build doesn’t feel cheap, but there is a small amount of flex and bend, particularly on the bottom plate.

The 14-inch, 2K touchscreen OLED display, however, is the first thing you notice and its standout feature. For a $649 device, it offers vivid contrast and good color separation. It’s quite a glossy display, however, so you’ll probably find yourself repositioning it as I did during my testing. At 300 nits of brightness, it won’t look great outdoors, but the 2K resolution is crisp enough to run Windows at higher resolutions.

The OmniBook 5 also addresses one of the Neo’s biggest drawbacks: the lack of an HDMI port. Here, you’ve got one on the laptop’s left side, along with two USB-C (not Thunderbolt) ports and an audio jack. But sorry, you’ll have to do without a USB-A.

Also: My week with latest Googlebooks: The good, the bad, and the promising.

According to recent reports, the crisp display, bright colors, and responsive keyboard and trackpad all work together to make this laptop feel premium and enjoyable to use — addressing the main complaints consumers typically had of budget Windows PCs: that they’re thick and bulky with uninspiring builds and dingy displays. For $649, you’re looking at a much better-looking laptop that actually has some character. But how does it perform?

Here is where the trade-offs become a little more evident. The HP OmniBook 5 comes with an Intel Core 5 Series 3 processor — a step below its “Ultra” lineup of consumer chips, emphasizing battery life over power. The starting configuration at $649 also comes with 8GB of RAM, the bare minimum I’d suggest in 2027, with the 16GB model starting at $899.

It’s a good price, but 8GB of memory in Windows is not the same as 8GB in MacOS. This isn’t just conjecture; even Microsoft knew this was the case, as evidenced by its recent changes to speed and memory improvements in Windows 11. The OmniBook 5 I was given for testing was the 16GB model, but I have tested other devices with 8GB of memory, and there are still performance limitations.

Industry observers note that I’d suggest the 8GB model for owners who only need to handle the basics on this device: checking email, browsing the web, and working with office and productivity software. With 16GB, you’ll have a lot more options, including creative tasks like photo and video editing — even some gaming. I ran “WoW Forever” (a latest game that’s not especially graphically intensive) on the OmniBook 5 with max graphics settings — it played surprisingly well, with bright colors popping on the OLED panel.

When it comes to raw power, this laptop performs similarly to its competitors, emphasizing longevity and battery life, making a solid option for students, teens, and everyday consumers. For pros and creators looking for more horsepower to run intensive workflows, HP has plenty of other options, such as the aforementioned HP OmniBook X Flip 14 or the HP EliteBook 8 G1a on the higher end.

Also: The best laptops: Expert tested and reviewed.

According to recent reports, speaking of longevity, battery life is fantastic, with the OmniBook 5 lasting just about the entire workday on one charge — and that’s after multiple calls throughout the day. The better-than-expected battery life is due to HP pairing a large 60Whr cell with the Intel Core 5 — a very power-efficient chip. HP cites up to 42 hours during its video playback test, but I’d expect an average of 8-10 hours of regular use on one charge.

According to recent reports, even better is the 60Wh mini GaN wall charger, which looks like it should power your smartphone — not your laptop. This tiny charger makes the OmniBook 5 even easier to commute with, adding almost no weight or bulk to the total package.

One last thing to note about this laptop is the very limited on-board storage, which solidifies its use case as a cloud-first laptop for the basics. The 8GB configuration starts with a 256GB SSD, upgradable to 512GB — which is the minimum I’d suggest in 2026, especially on a Windows PC. At 256GB, you’ll just be especially limited with the apps you can install, reducing the laptop’s longevity over time.

Sources indicate that compared to the MacBook Neo, the HP OmniBook 5 offers 60% more battery capacity, an HDMI port, a backlit keyboard, and a touchscreen OLED display for the same price. However, 8GB of RAM in Windows is a little more limiting than 8GB of RAM in MacOS, and there’s no way around it. This is not a dig on the OmniBook 5, it’s just the reality of Windows 11.

According to recent reports, also: Want the best Wi-Fi laptop? We tested 7 models.

According to recent reports, performance for the tasks it’s designed for is quite good, but you need to be confident your intended use case doesn’t extend into more demanding tasks or require several hundred gigs of storage for large apps. The HP OmniBook 5 is a colorful, solid “budget premium” laptop that addresses the MacBook Neo’s trade-offs, but makes its own in the process.

Some of the most popular Android smartwatches just got a battery-saving update. Google released an updated version of Google Play Services on Tuesday that can help extend the battery life of a Wear OS smartwatch.

The v26.45 update concerns location tracking during outdoor workouts. Wear OS smartwatch users can now use their phone’s Global Navigation Satellite System to track their location during an outdoor workout, which can conserve battery life by outsourcing the smartwatch’s energy to the smartphone when it isn’t in Battery Saver mode.

Sources indicate that also: Pixel Watch 4 vs. Watch 5: Is Google’s new model worth it?

Constantly communicating with satellites during an outdoor workout can be a battery drain, and every minute of battery life counts when you use your smartwatch for communication, workout tracking, and health monitoring. GPS services, a bright, always-on display, and continuous health sensors like SpO2 can squeeze the most juice out of your smartwatch.

Sources indicate that wear OS software is used by many of the most popular smartwatch brands, including Google, Samsung, and OnePlus. Both the Google Pixel Watch and Samsung Galaxy Watch’s largest batteries last approximately 40 hours. That’s nearly two days of use from two top Android smartwatches, but you’d be surprised how promptly it can drain.

Also: Galaxy Watch 9 review: Health data overload, but built for the future.

The patch improves battery life without users having to take any action or change any settings — the Google Play Services version 26.45 works quietly under the hood.

That’s not the only Google Play Services revision that Wear OS smartwatch owners can take advantage of. Another recent update lets users view on their phone a larger preview of any watch face they want to install on their smartwatch.

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.

Industry observers note that aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

#5005. Breaking: Flowtica Verso vs. the Note Pro: Does an AI voice recorder need a screen? I say no, here’s why

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1529 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Zdnet ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Flowtica Verso vs. the Note Pro: Does an AI voice recorder need a screen? I say no, here’s why

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1529 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Zdnet

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that we primarily interact with AI via our phones and computers, but there’s a growing subset of devices that act as a go-between.
  • Also: The Flowtica Verso AI notetaker is my upcoming favorite MagSafe gadget.
  • Sources indicate that the Verso is a standalone device, but it also has a MagSafe connector so you can attach it to the back of your smartphone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that we primarily interact with AI via our phones and computers, but there’s a growing subset of devices that act as a go-between. The upcoming Flowtica Verso is one such device. And it’s got something that’s new to this class of device — a significant touchscreen display.

Also: The Flowtica Verso AI notetaker is my upcoming favorite MagSafe gadget.

Sources indicate that the Verso is a standalone device, but it also has a MagSafe connector so you can attach it to the back of your smartphone. Yes, that means yet another screen, which can be a lot to ask. I recently tested the Verso to see if it does what it says.

Industry observers note that I’m old enough to have been taught a bunch of now obsolete skills, shorthand being one. Another skill that’s come and gone is dictation and transcription. I owned several recorders over the years — from tape to digital — and used them extensively.

I use them, however, because a close encounter with a disease-ridden Scottish tick left me with a bit of cramping and neuropathy in my hands, ultimately nudging me toward investigating more non-keyboard options for my phone.

Industry observers note that aside from being potential time-savers, AI voice recorders are a next-generation accessibility solution. After all, we’re all one misfortune away from needing something to make the digital world more accessible.

I’ve tried quite a few AI voice recorders, and to date my favorite has been the Comulytic Note Pro, which doesn’t have the Verso’s big e-paper display and right now costs $130. I’ve used this more than I thought I would, but I have to admit that it still hasn’t integrated itself into my workflow in a way that makes it a must-have.

Also: I cloned my voice with free AI tools – and tested a scam call on my family.

Now that I’ve used both for a while, I think I can offer some grist for the mill for anyone on the fence about whether they want an AI voice recorder with or without an e-paper touchscreen.

It has been revealed that the Flowtica Verso is the latest AI notetaker I’ve tested, but another good one is Comulytic’s Note Pro, a device I reviewed favorably earlier this year. Both devices are excellent. Despite the Verso having twice as many microphones as the Note Pro (four compared to two, plus a dedicated conduction mic for recording phone calls), I can’t fault either of them. Try as I might, I really can’t find a significant difference in recording quality between the two.

According to recent reports, the Comulytic Note Pro is smaller, thinner, and lighter, and feels more like a finder card than a recorder. There’s a button to start recording and a tiny 0.8-inch LCD status display to keep you in the loop. And it offers a quite decent battery life of 45 hours (and 107 days on standby). The Note Pro is simple; all you need to worry about is keeping it charged and pressing the button to start recording.

I want to like the Verso. It’s a nice bit of hardware with a premium, durable feel, and it comes packed with the promise of making my life easier. And some aspects of the device work well. Its voice pickup — even when multiple people are talking — is unnervingly accurate, and the transcription is excellent.

Also: My 3 favorite AI tools for voice dictation while vibe coding.

It’s also very good at recording phone conversations, though I noticed that using a phone case can reduce accuracy. I’m assuming that this gives the conduction mic, which uses vibration to pick up the other side of phone conversations, less to go on. Battery life is excellent as well, and I have no problem believing Flowtica’s 70-hour runtime claim.

Industry observers note that the Verso is slow. Really, painfully slow.

In a recent development, with the Note Pro, you press a button, and off you go. With the Verso, there’s a noticeable lag as you sit there waiting for the screen to refresh and the action to kick off.

Also: 5 ways I use ChatGPT Work to save time and money.

It has been revealed that E-paper always has a lag, but this goes beyond that. I first found out how frustrating this lag was when I needed to enter a 16-character Wi-Fi passcode. Switching from uppercase to lowercase was tedious, and the delay when switching the keyboard to numeric mode made me think it wasn’t working properly. It was; I just wasn’t giving it time before jabbing some more.

This lag also reduced my ability to read transcriptions on the device. It was quicker, easier, and less frustrating to look at them on my iPhone because using the Verso’s display felt like going back to an old Kindle Paperwhite (in a bad way).

This slowness never got better, and I never got used to it. As a result, it undermines the usefulness of the touchscreen as both a display and a user input method. This is a shame because it’s a really neat feature that might keep me off my phone more, but that half-second delay between tap and reaction was too much for me. That’s the way of it with devices that have to be power-efficient. Processing power is always the first thing to be sacrificed.

Also: I’ve owned 50+ power stations – one number matters most.

Bottom line: I found myself getting frustrated by how slow the Verso was, especially when tapping the screen or pressing the buttons. It all felt too hit-and-miss. The Note Pro might have been just as slow behind the scenes, but there was no display to give me that feedback. Also, everything was done either with a button press or through the app. And since I’ve always got my phone with me, this is no hardship.

Industry observers note that the Verso could also be simplified by removing the “Ask Flowtica” button. I don’t see the point of a separate physical button for a feature I already have on plenty of other devices. And to make things worse, it was painfully slow to use.

Also: 5 USB cables that can fry hardware and steal your data – or worse.

I could whip out my phone, open a browser, and type my question — and quite possibly another two or three — and get an answer while Flowtica was still thinking.

I also received a few “no internet connection” messages with the Verso, and no, my internet connection was fine (I did try it on several Wi-Fi networks, with similar results). Maybe these issues are specific to my device, or maybe they’ll be resolved with future software updates, but these connectivity dropouts certainly got in the way of using the Verso.

The Note Pro just worked. The one button did what it was supposed to do, and there were never any problems moving recordings from the device to the cloud for transcription.

There’s little point in spending money on an AI voice recorder if you’re not going to use AI to process that raw audio and output it as something useful.

Also: I tried a $200 smartwatch with voice recording – how it beat the Apple Watch.

Recent findings suggest that both devices come with unlimited transcription, but both companies put limits on how much of the “advanced” features you can use before you have to put skin in the game and buy a subscription. For the Verso, live on-screen transcription, Voice ID, and summaries are advanced features that are limited to 300 minutes a month for those not on a subscription blueprint.

If this feels somewhat confusing — and you’re not alone — the easiest way to think about it is that Comulytic’s free tier includes unlimited basic summaries, while Verso’s main screen feature is metered.

It has been revealed that the Flowtica Verso hits the market with a list price of $299. That’s a steep premium to pay for that e-paper display compared to the competition. And it feels even steeper when the lag gets in the way as much as it did.

The Comulytic Note Pro is under $130, which is about as cheap as it gets for a good AI voice recorder. Even the biggest name in the game, the Plaud Note Pro, is only $189.

Also: Google is making it easier to opt out of Gemini AI model training.

Industry observers note that if I didn’t feel like I was fighting the lag on almost everything I did with the Verso, I’d stick with it. But it’s frustrating, and it’s far easier to slip back into old habits. It’s possible future updates will streamline the Verso’s UI, but if you’re someone who finds it hard to wait half a second for something to happen, it could feel frustrating and is the reason why I’m sticking with the Note Pro for now.

Finally, be aware that subscriptions come into play on both devices, and that the Verso’s screen offers metered free usage for what it calls “AI minutes” before requiring a monthly payment.
